Evolution algebras: a survey of results and a list of open problems11 1 The work is supported by FCT 2023.08031.CEECIND and UID/00212/2025; by the Spanish Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovación 10.13039/501100011033, grants PID2023-152673NB-I00 and PID2023-149804NB-I00; by grant Fortalece 2023/03 of “Comunidad Autónoma de La Rioja”; and by the Junta de Andalucía through project PPRO-FQM336-G-2023 (FQM336-G-FEDER).22 2 The original concept, the initial list of problems and the overall framework were developed by I.K., C.M.G. and A.V. The AI system Aristotle (Harmonic, https://aristotle.harmonic.fun/) assisted the authors in the literature search, error verification, computer experiments and the formal verification in Lean of the new observations of Section 2.1.

Ivan Kaygorodov33 3 CMA-UBI, University of Beira Interior, Covilhã, Portugal; kaygorodov.ivan@gmail.com, Cándido Martín González44 4 Departamento de Álgebra, Geometría y Topología, Universidad de Málaga, Málaga, Spain; candido_m@uma.es & Antonio Viruel55 5 Departamento de Álgebra, Geometría y Topología, Universidad de Málaga, Málaga, Spain; viruel@uma.es

Abstract: Evolution algebras, introduced by J. P. Tian as an algebraic model of non-Mendelian inheritance, are commutative algebras with a basis whose distinct elements multiply to zero. The first part of the paper surveys the theory: low-dimensional classifications, structure theory, nilpotency, automorphisms and derivations, directed graphs and random walks, infinite-dimensional and dynamical aspects, and embedding theorems. The second part is a unified list of fifty open questions and eleven new conjectures, each accompanied by the available evidence; two of the conjectures and one of the questions are settled here. We also prove several new observations, most of them formally verified in the proof assistant Lean (see Section 2.1.11): every finite group is the automorphism group of a simple evolution algebra over every field, and |Aut⁡(A)|/dimA|\Aut(A)|/\dim A takes every positive rational value on simple evolution algebras over every field; infinitude of the automorphism group of nilpotent algebras, the possible numbers of idempotents of real perfect evolution algebras, a Galois-theoretic criterion for the existence of idempotents in dimension two, the average number of idempotents over finite fields, and a perfect evolution algebra whose automorphism group is a non-split extension.

Keywords: evolution algebra, natural basis, directed graph, automorphism group scheme, nilpotent algebra, idempotent, open problems.

MSC2020: 17A60 (primary); 17D92, 05C25, 20B25, 14L15, 60J10 (secondary).

1 A survey of results

1.1 Introduction and basic notions

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be a field. A 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra AA is called an evolution algebra if it admits a basis B={ei}i∈ΛB=\{e_{i}\}_{i\in\Lambda}, called a natural basis, such that ei​ej=0e_{i}e_{j}=0 whenever i≠ji\neq j. Evolution algebras are commutative, and in general they are neither associative nor power-associative. If Λ={1,…,n}\Lambda=\{1,\dots,n\} and

ei2=∑j=1nωi​j​ej,e_{i}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\omega_{ij}e_{j},

the matrix MB=(ωi​j)M_{B}=(\omega_{ij}) is the structure matrix of AA relative to BB. Conversely, every square matrix is the structure matrix of an evolution algebra, so an nn-dimensional evolution algebra is the same thing as a square matrix modulo the action of changes of natural basis. The map ei↦ei2e_{i}\mapsto e_{i}^{2} extended linearly is the evolution operator LBL_{B}. To AA and BB one attaches the directed graph Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) with vertex set Λ\Lambda and an arrow i→ji\to j whenever ωi​j≠0\omega_{ij}\neq 0 [48]; this graph is the single most useful tool of the theory.

Several classes of evolution algebras play a distinguished role. An evolution algebra is non-degenerate if ei2≠0e_{i}^{2}\neq 0 for every element of a natural basis; this does not depend on the natural basis, and it is equivalent to Ann⁡(A)=0\Ann(A)=0 [22]. It is perfect (also called idempotent or regular) if A2=AA^{2}=A; for finite-dimensional algebras this means that MBM_{B} is invertible. The basic rigidity phenomenon is that a perfect finite-dimensional evolution algebra has a unique natural basis up to permutation and non-zero scalars [48]; consequently its graph is an invariant of the algebra and its automorphisms are monomial. In general, a non-perfect algebra may have many essentially different natural bases (for instance, the zero algebra has all bases as natural bases), and the corresponding graphs need not be isomorphic.

We use the following conventions throughout. Unless stated otherwise, algebras are finite-dimensional. An element u=∑ixi​eiu=\sum_{i}x_{i}e_{i} is an idempotent if and only if

xj=∑iωi​j​xi2(j=1,…,n),x_{j}=\sum_{i}\omega_{ij}x_{i}^{2}\qquad(j=1,\dots,n), (1)

a system of nn quadratic equations in nn unknowns. The lower powers are

A1=AA^{1}=A, Ak=∑i+j=kAi​AjA^{k}=\sum_{i+j=k}A^{i}A^{j},

and AA is nilpotent of index kk if Ak=0≠Ak−1A^{k}=0\neq A^{k-1}. The derived series is

A(1)=A2A^{(1)}=A^{2}, A(m+1)=(A(m))2A^{(m+1)}=(A^{(m)})^{2},

and A(∞)A^{(\infty)} denotes its stable term. We write 𝐀𝐮𝐭⁡(A)\mathbf{Aut}(A) for the affine group scheme of automorphisms and Aut⁡(A)=𝐀𝐮𝐭​(A)​(𝕜)\Aut(A)=\mathbf{Aut}(A)(\Bbbk).

Example 1.

If ei2=eie_{i}^{2}=e_{i} for all ii, then A≅𝕜nA\cong\Bbbk^{n} is the associative algebra of functions on nn points; it has 2n2^{n} idempotents and Aut⁡(A)≅Sn\Aut(A)\cong S_{n}.

Example 2.

The algebra with ei2=ei+1e_{i}^{2}=e_{i+1} (indices modulo nn) is perfect and its graph is an oriented nn-cycle. Its diagonal automorphisms are ei↦t2i−1​eie_{i}\mapsto t^{2^{i-1}}e_{i} with t2n−1=1t^{2^{n}-1}=1, and Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) has order n⁡(2n−1)n(2^{n}-1).

Example 3.

If e12=e2e_{1}^{2}=e_{2} and e22=0e_{2}^{2}=0, the algebra is nilpotent of index 33; its graph is a single arrow, and the algebra has infinitely many automorphisms.

Five basic results

The following statements are used throughout the paper; they are the backbone of the finite-dimensional theory.

Theorem 4 (Elduque–Labra [48]).

If AA is a perfect finite-dimensional evolution algebra and {ei}\{e_{i}\}, {fi}\{f_{i}\} are natural bases, then there are a permutation σ\sigma and scalars ti∈𝕜×t_{i}\in\Bbbk^{\times} with fi=ti​eσ⁡(i)f_{i}=t_{i}e_{\sigma(i)}. In particular Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) does not depend on BB up to isomorphism, every automorphism of AA is monomial, and Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) is finite.

Theorem 5 ([36, 30, 48]).

For a finite-dimensional evolution algebra AA the following are equivalent: AA is nil (with respect to the principal powers xk+1=xk​xx^{k+1}=x^{k}x; see Proposition 9 for plenary powers); AA is right nilpotent; AA is nilpotent; for some (equivalently, every) natural basis BB the graph Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) has no oriented cycles; in some natural basis the structure matrix is strictly upper triangular. The nilpotency index of an nn-dimensional nilpotent evolution algebra is at most 2n−1+12^{n-1}+1, and this bound is attained.

Theorem 6 (Cabrera Casado–Siles Molina–Velasco [22]).

A non-degenerate evolution algebra is the direct sum of irreducible evolution ideals, uniquely up to order; the summands correspond to the connected components of the underlying undirected graph of Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B). A finite-dimensional evolution algebra is simple if and only if it is perfect and Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) is strongly connected.

Theorem 7 (Elduque–Labra [50]).

For a perfect finite-dimensional evolution algebra the automorphism group scheme is an extension of a constant group of permutations of the vertices of the graph by a finite diagonalisable group scheme 𝐃\mathbf{D}, both determined by the graph; see (2) below. In particular Der⁡(A)=0\Der(A)=0 if char⁡𝕜∈{0,2}\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\in\{0,2\}.

Theorem 8 (Costoya–Ligouras–Tocino–Viruel [43]).

For every field 𝕜\Bbbk and every finite group GG there are infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic perfect evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebras AA with Aut⁡(A)≅G\Aut(A)\cong G.

A short chronology

The history of the subject can be summarised as follows. The notion was introduced in 2006 [113] and systematised in Tian’s 2008 monograph [111]. Between 2010 and 2014 Rozikov, Omirov, Ladra and their coauthors connected evolution algebras with population dynamics, Gibbs measures, chains and dibaric algebras [106, 34, 79, 74, 80], and the first structural results (nilpotency, derivations, classification in dimension two) appeared [30, 31, 35, 36]. In 2015–2017 three foundational contributions changed the landscape: the graph-theoretic viewpoint and the uniqueness of natural bases for perfect algebras [48, 49], the structure theory in arbitrary dimension [22] and the classification in dimension three [23]; at the same time nilpotent algebras were classified in low dimension [64] and gonosomal and isotopic viewpoints were introduced [115, 51]. From 2019 onwards automorphism group schemes [50], universality [43, 109], random walks on graphs [25, 26], Hilbert evolution algebras [118] and the systematic study of ideals through graphs [19, 9] became central, and a historical survey appeared [38]. The most recent work concerns non-degenerate algebras [29], counting over finite fields [119], lattices of subalgebras [75, 77, 78, 76], deformations [83], idempotents and solvability [58, 66], Grothendieck rings [1] and embeddings of commutative algebras [42].

The first part of the paper surveys what is known. We have tried to be complete with respect to the main lines of research, but the literature is large and we apologise for any omission. Further general accounts are the monograph of Tian [111], the historical survey of Ceballos, Falcón, Núñez-Valdés and Tenorio [38], the short survey [112], and the general survey on classification problems for non-associative structures [69] and its geometric counterpart [70]. The second part contains the open questions and conjectures, together with a number of new observations.

1.2 Origins: genetics, Markov chains and Tian’s programme

Evolution algebras were introduced by Tian and Vojtěchovský [113] and developed systematically in Tian’s monograph [111]. The motivation comes from non-Mendelian genetics: in asexual (uniparental) inheritance, for instance of organelle genes, a gamete of type eie_{i} reproduces by “self-crossing”, and the offspring distribution is encoded by ei2=∑jωi​j​eje_{i}^{2}=\sum_{j}\omega_{ij}e_{j}, while distinct gametes do not interact, which gives ei​ej=0e_{i}e_{j}=0. When the rows of MBM_{B} are probability vectors, the evolution operator is the transition operator of a discrete-time Markov chain, and Tian interpreted the basic notions of Markov chains in algebraic terms: persistent and transient generators, communication classes, periodicity and absorption. He proved a hierarchical (“semi-direct”) decomposition of an evolution algebra into simple components and transient spaces, related algebraic periods to the periods of Markov chains, and introduced the evolution algebra of a graph, defined by the adjacency matrix. He also gave applications to the population genetics of organelle heredity and to the analysis of Markov processes. These foundational ideas, collected in [111] and in the programmatic paper [112], set the agenda for much of the later work.

Soon afterwards evolution algebras were connected with other parts of mathematical biology and statistical mechanics. Rozikov and Tian [106] associated evolution algebras with Gibbs measures on graphs, and Ladra and Rozikov introduced the evolution algebra of a bisexual population [79], a non-baric but dibaric algebra; see also [74] for the connections with dibaric algebras and population genetics, the “chicken population” algebras [80, 46, 105] and the constrained algebras of [47]. Varro generalised the bisexual construction to gonosomal algebras, which model sex determination systems [115]. Further models include mosquito populations [107] and pulse processes in networks [2].

1.3 Classification in low dimension

1.3.1 Dimension two and three

Two-dimensional evolution algebras over ℂ\mathbb{C} were classified by Casas, Ladra, Omirov and Rozikov [36], who also described an algorithm deciding isomorphism of evolution algebras; real two-dimensional algebras were treated by Murodov [92] and by Bekbaev [4]. A geometric invariant, the “square” of a two-dimensional evolution algebra, was introduced in [33], where identities of degree at most four, derivations, automorphism group schemes and associative representations of all two-dimensional algebras are determined.

The three-dimensional case is substantially harder. Cabrera Casado, Siles Molina and Velasco classified three-dimensional evolution algebras over fields of characteristic different from 22 containing roots of orders 22, 33 and 77 [23]; the classification uses the graph, the dimension of A2A^{2} and the annihilator, and produces a long list including several parametric families. An alternative approach, based on chains of two-dimensional algebras and on the annihilator and socle stabilising indices, was developed in [7], and a classification adapted to dimensions two and three over arbitrary fields appears in [40]. Simple evolution algebras of dimensions two and three were classified over arbitrary fields in [18], using the graph, moduli sets, inductive limit groups and the Zariski topology.

1.3.2 Higher dimensions and special classes

Four-dimensional perfect non-simple evolution algebras were classified in [15], with the isomorphism problem completed in [3]. Evolution algebras with one-dimensional square were classified by means of inner product spaces [84]: if dimA2=1\dim A^{2}=1 and aa generates A2A^{2}, then x​y=⟨x,y⟩​axy=\langle x,y\rangle a for a symmetric bilinear form, and three broad classes appear according to the position of aa. Calderón, Fernández Ouaridi and Kaygorodov [29] attached to every non-degenerate evolution algebra an invariant consisting of an ordered sequence of lower-dimensional evolution algebras from a specific family; it yields a classification method for non-degenerate evolution algebras, carried out up to dimension three, and descriptions of derivations and of the variety of evolution algebras with square of dimension at most one. Power-associative evolution algebras are Jordan algebras and admit a Wedderburn decomposition; they are classified up to dimension six [96].

1.3.3 Isotopy

Isotopisms of evolution algebras correspond to mutations of genotypes. Falcón, Falcón and Núñez showed, using computational algebraic geometry, that there are exactly four (strong) isotopism classes of two-dimensional evolution algebras over any field [51], and determined the isotopism classes of three-dimensional ones [52]. Ternary derivations and the group scheme of ternary automorphisms of perfect evolution algebras were computed in [85].

1.3.4 Counting

Isomorphism classes of perfect nn-dimensional evolution algebras correspond to orbits of the semidirect product Sn⋉(𝕜×)nS_{n}\ltimes(\Bbbk^{\times})^{n} acting on invertible structure matrices. Wei and Zou [119] turned this into a counting problem over finite fields, derived a general counting formula and obtained explicit formulas for n≤4n\leq 4.

1.3.5 Recognising evolution algebras

Deciding whether a given algebra is an evolution algebra amounts to deciding whether nn symmetric matrices describing the product are simultaneously diagonalisable by congruence (the SDC problem) [6]; necessary and sufficient conditions for simultaneous orthogonalisation of families of inner products over arbitrary fields were given in [13]. In [6] it is also shown that classical genetic algebras of Mendelian and auto-tetraploid inheritance are not evolution algebras but are limits of evolution algebras. Imomkulov and Rozikov [67] approximated an arbitrary algebra by the family of evolution algebras given by the Jacobians of its evolution operator.

1.4 Structure theory

1.4.1 Subalgebras, ideals and decompositions

Evolution subalgebras and evolution ideals (those having a natural basis that extends to a natural basis of the algebra) behave much better than arbitrary subalgebras and ideals. Cabrera Casado, Siles Molina and Velasco developed the theory in arbitrary dimension [22]: they described ideals generated by one element, characterised simple evolution algebras, proved that a non-degenerate evolution algebra is irreducible if and only if its graph is connected, and established existence and uniqueness of a decomposition of a non-degenerate algebra into irreducible components (the fragmentation process); uniqueness fails in the degenerate case. Basic ideals were introduced and studied in [14]. Boudi, Cabrera Casado and Siles Molina [5] introduced the evolution rank, proved that in a non-degenerate algebra every family of natural orthogonal vectors extends to a natural basis, showed that ideals of perfect evolution algebras are basic, and located nilpotent elements of order three through principal minors of the structure matrix.

The relation between ideals and the graph was made precise in [19]: there is a monotone Galois connection between absorption ideals and hereditary saturated subsets of vertices, which describes maximal ideals and absorption ideals combinatorially and characterises finitely generated evolution algebras under suitable graph conditions. The intersection 𝔐⁡(A)\mathfrak{M}(A) of all maximal ideals and a subdirect-product structure theorem were studied in [21]. The absorption radical can be read off from the acyclic vertices of the graph [24], and the reductive radical was introduced in [20]. Cabrera Casado et al. [9] related non-degeneracy, zero annihilator, the absorption property, von Neumann regularity and primeness to properties of the family of all graphs of AA, showed that primeness is equivalent (under semiprimeness) to downward directedness of the graphs, proved that semiprimeness and perfection cannot be characterised combinatorially, and described the centroid as the functions constant along connected components. Peirce decompositions relative to idempotents were studied by Paniello [98].

Arbitrary subalgebras of evolution algebras need not be evolution algebras [32]. Camacho, Khudoyberdiyev and Omirov classified the nilpotent evolution algebras all of whose subalgebras are evolution subalgebras with extendable natural bases, and formulated conjectures for the non-nilpotent case [32]; two of them were proved by García-Martínez and Pérez-Rodríguez [58]. Ladra and Pérez-Rodríguez proved that subalgebras of perfect (regular) evolution algebras are evolution algebras, and characterised the existence of subalgebras of codimension one [77]. The subalgebra lattice was investigated in [75] (distributivity in the nilpotent case, modularity of solvable algebras with maximal index of solvability) and in [78], where modular evolution algebras are fully characterised in the nilpotent case and among supersolvable regular algebras. A Frattini theory, based on the supersolvable nilradical, was developed in [76]. Order-theoretic structures on substructures and the socle of an evolution algebra were studied by González Nevado [62].

1.4.2 Radicals and spectra

Velasco described the maximal modular ideals and the Jacobson radical of an evolution algebra and introduced two notions of spectrum of an element, computed via the eigenvalues of suitable matrices built from the structure constants [116]. Analytic aspects (Banach algebra norms, continuity of the evolution operator) were studied by Mellon and Velasco [86].

1.4.3 Idempotents and solvability

The idempotents of an evolution algebra are the solutions of (1). For algebras coming from biological models they are the equilibrium states of the population and were computed in many concrete cases, see e.g. [79, 47, 94]. García-Martínez and Pérez-Rodríguez [58] analysed the solution set of the generic system by elementary algebraic geometry: every perfect complex evolution algebra has a non-zero idempotent. They conjectured that a complex evolution algebra is solvable if and only if it has no non-zero idempotents. One implication is clear, since an idempotent lies in every term of the derived series. Hu and Wen [66] found a three-dimensional counterexample to the other implication (an isomorphic algebra appears in [42, Remark 3.9], as an evolution envelope of a two-dimensional algebra); it is the exceptional member of a one-parameter family, and they proved the equivalence whenever A(∞)A^{(\infty)} is itself an evolution algebra. Resolubility of evolution algebras was also studied in [54].

1.4.4 The evolution operator

The evolution operator depends on the natural basis. Its behaviour, the set of all evolution operators of an algebra, and the algebras whose evolution operator is an endomorphism were studied by Fernández-Ternero, Gómez-Sousa and Núñez-Valdés [53, 55].

1.5 Nilpotency

Nilpotency was the first structural property to be understood. Casas, Ladra, Omirov and Rozikov proved that nil, right nilpotent and nilpotent finite-dimensional evolution algebras are exactly those whose structure matrix is strictly upper triangular in a suitable natural basis [36]. Camacho, Gómez, Omirov and Turdibaev characterised nilpotency by matrix properties and proved that the maximal nilpotency index of an nn-dimensional evolution algebra is 2n−1+12^{n-1}+1 [30]; algebras with maximal index were characterised and classified in [35], where wide classes with index 2n−s+12^{n-s}+1 are also constructed. Elduque and Labra gave the conceptual statement: an evolution algebra is nilpotent if and only if Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) has no oriented cycles [48].

Classification of some classes of nilpotent evolution algebras proceeds by annihilator extensions [64]. Hegazi and Abdelwahab classified nilpotent evolution algebras up to dimension four over arbitrary fields [64] and in dimension five over algebraically closed fields [65]. Elduque and Labra [49] pointed out a subtle gap in the extension method (a natural basis of a quotient need not lift to a natural basis), introduced the type and further invariants attached to the upper annihilating series, constructed families of nilpotent evolution algebras from non-degenerate symmetric bilinear forms and commuting symmetric endomorphisms, and completed the classification up to dimension five over algebraically closed fields of characteristic different from two. Derivations, automorphisms, local and 22-local derivations of nilpotent evolution algebras of maximal nilindex were determined in [89], the group exp⁡(Der⁡(E))\exp(\Der(E)) was shown to be a normal subgroup of Aut⁡(E)\Aut(E) of computable index in [90], and tensor products of nilpotent evolution algebras were studied in [100]. Rota–Baxter operators of weights 00 and 11 on nilpotent algebras of maximal nilindex were classified in [101], and local Rota–Baxter operators of weight zero in [102]. Formal deformations of evolution algebras and the degenerations among nilpotent evolution algebras of dimension at most four were determined by Makhlouf and Pérez-Rodríguez [83]; see [70] for a survey of the geometric classification of non-associative algebras.

In infinite dimension the situation changes: Tian and Zou constructed finitely generated evolution algebras (over rings with nilpotent elements) which are nil but not nilpotent [114], and nil and nilpotent are not equivalent for Hilbert evolution algebras [28].

In finite dimension, the word “nil” in Theorem 5 has to be understood with respect to the principal powers xk+1=xk​xx^{k+1}=x^{k}x: for the plenary powers x[1]=xx^{[1]}=x, x[m+1]=(x[m])2x^{[m+1]}=(x^{[m]})^{2}, nil and nilpotent are not equivalent even in finite dimension, as the following example, based on the evolution envelopes of [42], shows.

Proposition 9.

Over every field 𝕜\Bbbk there is a 1515-dimensional evolution algebra EE which is not nilpotent and satisfies (x2)2=0(x^{2})^{2}=0, that is x[3]=0x^{[3]}=0, for every x∈Ex\in E. In particular, EE is nil of bounded index with respect to plenary powers, and, by Theorem 5, it is not nil with respect to principal powers.

Proof.

Let SS be the commutative algebra of Suttles [110], with basis a1,…,a5a_{1},\dots,a_{5} and non-zero products a1​a2=a2​a4=−a1​a5=a3a_{1}a_{2}=a_{2}a_{4}=-a_{1}a_{5}=a_{3}, a1​a3=a4a_{1}a_{3}=a_{4}, a2​a3=a5a_{2}a_{3}=a_{5} (and the symmetric ones). Then S2=span⁡{a3,a4,a5}S^{2}=\mathrm{span}\{a_{3},a_{4},a_{5}\} and S2​S2=0S^{2}S^{2}=0. Moreover, SS is not nilpotent: if a3∈Ska_{3}\in S^{k}, then a4=a1​a3a_{4}=a_{1}a_{3} and a5=a2​a3a_{5}=a_{2}a_{3} lie in Sk+1S^{k+1} and a3=a2​a4∈Sk+2a_{3}=a_{2}a_{4}\in S^{k+2}; since a3∈S2a_{3}\in S^{2}, we get a3∈Ska_{3}\in S^{k} for all k≥2k\geq 2.

We use the evolution envelope of [42] in the following explicit form, valid in every characteristic. Write mi​j=ai​aj=mj​im_{ij}=a_{i}a_{j}=m_{ji} and, for s=∑isi​ais=\sum_{i}s_{i}a_{i}, consider the linear forms λi​(s)=si\lambda_{i}(s)=s_{i} (1≤i≤5)(1\leq i\leq 5) and λi​j​(s)=si+sj\lambda_{ij}(s)=s_{i}+s_{j} (1≤i<j≤5)(1\leq i<j\leq 5). Since (si+sj)​(ti+tj)−si​ti−sj​tj=si​tj+sj​ti(s_{i}+s_{j})(t_{i}+t_{j})-s_{i}t_{i}-s_{j}t_{j}=s_{i}t_{j}+s_{j}t_{i}, we have, for all s,t∈Ss,t\in S,

s​t=∑iλi​(s)​λi​(t)​vi+∑i<jλi​j​(s)​λi​j​(t)​mi​j,vi=mi​i−∑j≠imi​j.st=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}(s)\lambda_{i}(t)\,v_{i}+\sum_{i<j}\lambda_{ij}(s)\lambda_{ij}(t)\,m_{ij},\qquad v_{i}=m_{ii}-\sum_{j\neq i}m_{ij}.

Let EE be the evolution algebra with natural basis {fi}i∪{fi​j}i<j\{f_{i}\}_{i}\cup\{f_{ij}\}_{i<j}, let ι:S→E\iota\colon S\to E be the injective linear map ι⁡(s)=∑iλi​(s)​fi+∑i<jλi​j​(s)​fi​j\iota(s)=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}(s)f_{i}+\sum_{i<j}\lambda_{ij}(s)f_{ij}, and put fi2=ι⁡(vi)f_{i}^{2}=\iota(v_{i}), fi​j2=ι⁡(mi​j)f_{ij}^{2}=\iota(m_{ij}). The displayed identity gives ι⁡(s)​ι​(t)=ι⁡(s​t)\iota(s)\iota(t)=\iota(st), so ι⁡(S)≅S\iota(S)\cong S is a subalgebra of EE (in fact an ideal, as fi​ι​(s)=λi​(s)​fi2f_{i}\iota(s)=\lambda_{i}(s)f_{i}^{2} and fi​j​ι​(s)=λi​j​(s)​fi​j2f_{ij}\iota(s)=\lambda_{ij}(s)f_{ij}^{2} lie in ι⁡(S)\iota(S)). Since ι⁡(S)\iota(S) is not nilpotent, neither is EE. Finally, E2E^{2} is spanned by the elements fi2,fi​j2f_{i}^{2},f_{ij}^{2}, which lie in ι⁡(S2)\iota(S^{2}); hence for x∈Ex\in E we have x2=ι⁡(s)x^{2}=\iota(s) with s∈S2s\in S^{2}, and (x2)2=ι⁡(s2)=0(x^{2})^{2}=\iota(s^{2})=0 because S2​S2=0S^{2}S^{2}=0. ∎

More generally, the same argument shows that if a commutative algebra SS is nil of bounded index with respect to plenary powers but not nilpotent (as Suttles’ algebra, or ad-hoc examples in characteristic 22), then so is its evolution envelope, since x2∈Sx^{2}\in S for every element xx of the envelope. Compare with Question 15.

1.6 Automorphisms and derivations

1.6.1 Automorphism groups

Elduque and Labra proved that the automorphism group of a perfect evolution algebra is finite [48]. In [50] they showed that the affine group scheme of automorphisms of a perfect algebra sits in an exact sequence

1⟶𝐃⟶𝐀𝐮𝐭⁡(A)⟶𝐒,1\longrightarrow\mathbf{D}\longrightarrow\mathbf{Aut}(A)\longrightarrow\mathbf{S}, (2)

where 𝐃\mathbf{D} is a finite diagonalisable group scheme (the diagonal automorphisms with respect to the natural basis) and 𝐒\mathbf{S} is a constant group scheme of permutations of the vertices, both depending only on the graph. Costoya, Ligouras, Tocino and Viruel [43] constructed a faithful functor from finite simple graphs to perfect evolution algebras and proved that every finite group is the automorphism group of infinitely many perfect evolution algebras over any field (“evolution algebras are universally finite”), and that every constant finite group scheme is the automorphism group scheme of a perfect evolution algebra. Sriwongsa and Zou [109] gave another proof of universality, classified the nn-dimensional perfect algebras with Aut⁡(A)≅Sn\Aut(A)\cong S_{n} and those with maximal diagonal automorphism group. Costoya, Muñoz, Tocino and Viruel introduced Cayley evolution algebras and showed that every finite group is the automorphism group of an absolutely simple Cayley evolution algebra over every field with sufficiently many elements [45]; over arbitrary fields see Theorem 10 below. Costoya, Mayorga and Viruel [44] studied which permutation representations arise from (2): for k≥4k\geq 4 and nn large, proper kk-transitive subgroups of SnS_{n} never occur, whereas every permutation representation is realised on the set of natural idempotents of a suitable perfect algebra. Molinier [87] proved that every positive rational number is of the form |Aut⁡(A)|/dimA|\Aut(A)|/\dim A for a perfect evolution algebra AA.

The following construction shows that simplicity can be achieved over every field, which proves a conjecture of an earlier version of this text.

Theorem 10.

Let Δ\Delta be a finite strongly connected digraph without loops, with vertex set VV, |V|=m|V|=m. For every field 𝕜\Bbbk, let AΔA_{\Delta} be the evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra with natural basis {ev,ev′}v∈V\{e_{v},e^{\prime}_{v}\}_{v\in V} and

ev2=ev+∑v→wew+ev′,(ev′)2=ev(v∈V),e_{v}^{2}=e_{v}+\sum_{v\to w}e_{w}+e^{\prime}_{v},\qquad(e^{\prime}_{v})^{2}=e_{v}\qquad(v\in V),

the sum running over the arrows of Δ\Delta starting at vv. Then AΔA_{\Delta} is a simple evolution algebra of dimension 2​m2m, it remains simple after every extension of scalars, and Aut⁡(AΔ)≅Aut⁡(Δ)\Aut(A_{\Delta})\cong\Aut(\Delta). Consequently, every finite group is the automorphism group of a simple evolution algebra over every field.

Proof.

Ordering the basis as (ev)v∈V,(ev′)v∈V(e_{v})_{v\in V},(e^{\prime}_{v})_{v\in V}, the structure matrix is M=(I+NII0)M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I+N&I\\ I&0\end{smallmatrix}\right), where NN is the adjacency matrix of Δ\Delta. Exchanging the two block rows gives the block lower triangular matrix (I0I+NI)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&0\\ I+N&I\end{smallmatrix}\right), so detM=(−1)m≠0\det M=(-1)^{m}\neq 0 over every field, and AΔA_{\Delta} is perfect. Its graph consists of Δ\Delta, a loop at every eve_{v} and the 22-cycles ev⇄ev′e_{v}\rightleftarrows e^{\prime}_{v}; it is strongly connected, so AΔA_{\Delta} is simple by Theorem 6. Extending scalars does not change MM, hence AΔ⊗𝕜LA_{\Delta}\otimes_{\Bbbk}L is simple for every field extension L/𝕜L/\Bbbk.

By Theorem 4, every automorphism has the form φ⁡(ex)=tx​eσ⁡(x)\varphi(e_{x})=t_{x}e_{\sigma(x)} for a permutation σ\sigma of the basis indices and tx∈𝕜×t_{x}\in\Bbbk^{\times}, and φ​(ex)2=φ⁡(ex2)\varphi(e_{x})^{2}=\varphi(e_{x}^{2}) amounts to tx2​ωσ​x,σ​y=ty​ωx​yt_{x}^{2}\,\omega_{\sigma x,\sigma y}=t_{y}\,\omega_{xy} for all x,yx,y. Taking x=yx=y shows that σ\sigma maps vertices with a loop to vertices with a loop and vice versa, so σ\sigma preserves {ev}\{e_{v}\} and {ev′}\{e^{\prime}_{v}\}, and that tv2=tvt_{v}^{2}=t_{v}, i.e. tv=1t_{v}=1, for every v∈Vv\in V. For x=vx=v, y=wy=w in VV we get ωσ​v,σ​w=ωv​w\omega_{\sigma v,\sigma w}=\omega_{vw}, so τ=σ|V\tau=\sigma|_{V} is an automorphism of Δ\Delta. For x=vx=v, y=v′y=v^{\prime} we get ωσ​v,σ​v′=tv′≠0\omega_{\sigma v,\sigma v^{\prime}}=t_{v^{\prime}}\neq 0; the only primed vertex that receives an arrow from σ⁡(v)=τ⁡(v)\sigma(v)=\tau(v) is τ​(v)′\tau(v)^{\prime}, so σ⁡(v′)=τ​(v)′\sigma(v^{\prime})=\tau(v)^{\prime} and tv′=1t_{v^{\prime}}=1. Hence φ\varphi is the permutation automorphism ev↦eτ​ve_{v}\mapsto e_{\tau v}, ev′↦eτ​v′e^{\prime}_{v}\mapsto e^{\prime}_{\tau v}. Conversely every τ∈Aut⁡(Δ)\tau\in\Aut(\Delta) preserves the structure constants and so defines such an automorphism. Thus Aut⁡(AΔ)≅Aut⁡(Δ)\Aut(A_{\Delta})\cong\Aut(\Delta).

For the last statement, recall that every finite group GG is the automorphism group of a finite simple graph Γ\Gamma [56], which we may take connected (otherwise replace it by its complement). The symmetric digraph Δ\Delta with an arrow in each direction for every edge of Γ\Gamma is strongly connected and Aut⁡(Δ)=Aut⁡(Γ)≅G\Aut(\Delta)=\Aut(\Gamma)\cong G. ∎

Corollary 11.

For every field 𝕜\Bbbk and all positive integers p,qp,q there is a simple evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra AA with |Aut⁡(A)|/dimA=p/q|\Aut(A)|/\dim A=p/q.

Proof.

Choose N≥1N\geq 1 such that s=q​N​(2​p​N+1)−1−4​p​N−1≥1s=qN(2pN+1)-1-4pN-1\geq 1, and put a=2​p​Na=2pN, b=2​p​N+1b=2pN+1. Let Δ\Delta be the digraph with vertices hh, xix_{i} (i∈ℤa)(i\in\mathbb{Z}_{a}), yjy_{j} (j∈ℤb)(j\in\mathbb{Z}_{b}) and z1,…,zsz_{1},\dots,z_{s}, and arrows xi→xi+1x_{i}\to x_{i+1}, yj→yj+1y_{j}\to y_{j+1}, h⇄xih\rightleftarrows x_{i}, h⇄yjh\rightleftarrows y_{j}, h→z1→z2→…→zs→hh\to z_{1}\to z_{2}\to\dots\to z_{s}\to h. It is strongly connected and has 1+a+b+s=q​N​b1+a+b+s=qNb vertices. The vertex hh is the only one of out-degree a+b+1≥3a+b+1\geq 3, the zlz_{l} are the only vertices of out-degree 11 (and are fixed, since z1z_{1} is the only one of them receiving an arrow from hh), and removing these vertices leaves the disjoint union of an oriented aa-cycle and an oriented bb-cycle with a≠ba\neq b. Since hh is joined to all the xi,yjx_{i},y_{j} in both directions, every pair of rotations of the two cycles is an automorphism, and Aut⁡(Δ)≅ℤa×ℤb\Aut(\Delta)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{a}\times\mathbb{Z}_{b}. By Theorem 10, A=AΔA=A_{\Delta} is simple with |Aut⁡(A)|/dimA=a​b/(2​q​N​b)=p/q|\Aut(A)|/\dim A=ab/(2qNb)=p/q. ∎

Thus, Theorem 16(3) below holds over arbitrary fields and answers the analogue of Question 34 for simple evolution algebras.

Remark 12.

There is a variant of Theorem 10 based on cubic graphs. By [57], every finite group GG is the automorphism group of a connected 33-regular graph Γ\Gamma, with nn vertices, m=3​n/2m=3n/2 edges and incidence matrix BB. Let DD be the symmetric incidence digraph of Γ\Gamma (vertex set V⊔EV\sqcup E, with arrows v→ev\to e and e→ve\to v whenever v∈ev\in e), and add a loop of weight λ∈𝕜×\lambda\in\Bbbk^{\times} at every vertex, all other arrows having weight 11. The resulting structure matrix M⁡(λ)=(λ​InBBTλ​Im)M(\lambda)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda I_{n}&B\\ B^{T}&\lambda I_{m}\end{smallmatrix}\right) has determinant f⁡(λ)=λm−n​det(λ2​In−B​BT)f(\lambda)=\lambda^{m-n}\det(\lambda^{2}I_{n}-BB^{T}), a monic polynomial of degree n+mn+m. Since the vertices in VV have out-degree 44 and those in EE have out-degree 33, one has Aut⁡(D)≅Aut⁡(Γ)\Aut(D)\cong\Aut(\Gamma), and the argument of the proof above shows that the corresponding algebra is simple with automorphism group GG whenever f⁡(λ)≠0f(\lambda)\neq 0. Such a λ∈𝕜×\lambda\in\Bbbk^{\times} exists as soon as |𝕜|>2​n+1|\Bbbk|>2n+1; over small finite fields, however, it may not exist: for the Petersen graph (Aut⁡(Γ)≅S5\Aut(\Gamma)\cong S_{5}) the matrix B​BT=3​I+Adj⁡(Γ)BB^{T}=3I+\mathrm{Adj}(\Gamma) has the eigenvalue 11, so f⁡(λ)=0f(\lambda)=0 whenever λ2=1\lambda^{2}=1, in particular for every λ∈𝔽2×\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\times} and every λ∈𝔽3×\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{3}^{\times}. The pendant vertices ev′e^{\prime}_{v} in Theorem 10 avoid this problem, since there detM=±1\det M=\pm 1.

For infinite-dimensional algebras, the group of automorphisms that are diagonal with respect to a natural basis is an inverse limit of a diagram of groups indexed by the graph, and can be a dyadic solenoid [10]. Automorphisms of evolution algebras of graphs were related to graph symmetries in [103]. Hopf algebras representing 𝐀𝐮𝐭⁡(A)\mathbf{Aut}(A) for two-dimensional algebras were computed and compared with universal associative representations in [8]; there it is shown that Aut⁡(A)=1\Aut(A)=1 if and only if AA has no faithful associative commutative representation.

1.6.2 Derivations

Camacho, Gómez, Omirov and Turdibaev proved that Der⁡(A)=0\Der(A)=0 for complex evolution algebras with non-singular structure matrix and described derivations when the rank is n−1n-1 [31]. The exact sequence (2) shows that for perfect algebras Der⁡(A)=0\Der(A)=0 in characteristic 00 or 22, while in other characteristics Der⁡(A)\Der(A) is abelian and determined by the graph [50]. Derivations of evolution algebras of graphs were described in terms of the twin partition of the graph; for twin-free graphs the derivation algebra vanishes [12]. Non-degenerate algebras and Volterra evolution algebras (whose structure matrices are skew-symmetric, and which are connected to ergodicity of Volterra quadratic stochastic operators) were treated in [11], where loops of evolution algebras are introduced. Biderivations of some evolution algebras were considered in [97].

1.7 Graphs, random walks and combinatorics

The graph Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) was introduced by Elduque and Labra [48]; earlier, Camacho et al. [30] formulated planarity of graphs in terms of evolution algebras, and Tian [111] defined the evolution algebra of a graph. Systematic dictionaries between evolution algebras and (pseudo)digraphs were developed by Ceballos, Núñez and Tenorio [39, 37], by González-López and Núñez [61], and in the study of graphicable and S-graphicable algebras [95].

There are two natural evolution algebras attached to a finite graph GG: A⁡(G)A(G), whose structure matrix is the adjacency matrix, and AR​W​(G)A_{RW}(G), whose structure matrix is the transition matrix of the symmetric random walk. Cadavid, Rodiño Montoya and Rodríguez [25, 26] proved that they are always strongly isotopic, and that for non-singular graphs they are isomorphic if and only if GG is regular or biregular; they conjectured the same for singular graphs, and supporting families were given in [27]. The connection with Markov chains and statistics was explored in [82].

Tensor products of evolution algebras are evolution algebras, and the graph of the product relative to the product basis is the categorical product of the graphs. Inheritance of non-degeneracy, irreducibility, perfection and simplicity was studied in [17], where four-dimensional perfect algebras that are tensor products of two-dimensional ones are classified. Alshatnawi, Costoya and Viruel [1] studied the Grothendieck ring of finite-dimensional non-degenerate evolution algebras: they proved that the balance of the graph (the greatest common divisor of the balances of the cycles of the underlying undirected graph) is independent of the natural basis, that indecomposable factors of balance one cancel after tensoring while factors of larger balance produce zero-divisors, and they analysed the subring generated by cyclic algebras. Algebras attached to permutations were studied in [72, 94]. Giacomelli [59] introduced expander evolution algebras, whose graphs are expanders, and related the Cheeger constant with simplicity, subalgebras, growth and spectral gaps.

1.8 Infinite dimension, probability and dynamics

Many results above hold in arbitrary dimension [22, 19]. Hilbert evolution algebras, introduced by Vidal, Cadavid and Rodríguez [118], are Hilbert spaces with an orthonormal natural basis and a continuous product; they are naturally associated with discrete-time Markov chains with countable state space and with infinite graphs [117], and their nilpotency was analysed through weighted digraphs [28]. Coletti, de Lima and Luiz [41] constructed infinite-dimensional genetic and evolution algebras from Gibbs measures, with uncountable natural bases; infertility between macroscopically different configurations produces a decomposition into fertile ideals.

Casas, Ladra and Rozikov introduced chains of evolution algebras, families A[s,t]A^{[s,t]} whose structure matrices satisfy the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation [34]. Many examples in dimensions two and three, and the time behaviour of the baric property, of absolutely nilpotent elements and of idempotents, were studied in [104, 93, 105, 68, 73]; flows of arbitrary finite-dimensional algebras were introduced in [81]. Continuous evolution algebras arising from ordinary differential equations and flows on matrix Lie groups were introduced by Montaner and Paniello [88]. The quadratic evolution operator x↦x2x\mapsto x^{2} and its normalisations define discrete dynamical systems whose fixed points are idempotents; these were analysed for two-dimensional algebras [104] and for many biological models [79, 47, 107].

1.9 Embeddings, rings and further generalisations

Costoya, Fernández Ouaridi and Viruel [42] proved that every finite-dimensional commutative algebra is an ideal of a finite-dimensional evolution algebra, determined the smallest possible dimension of such an evolution algebra and, in characteristic different from two, related it to simultaneous Waring decompositions of the squaring map; for unital algebras the minimal dimension is the Waring rank of x↦x2x\mapsto x^{2}, which they computed for truncated polynomial algebras. It follows that the class of evolution algebras satisfies no polynomial identities other than the consequences of commutativity (see Remark 13 below). Evolution algebras over rings appear in [114] and, for free modules of rank two over domains, in [16], where quasiperfect algebras and coloured graphs are introduced. Isomorphism conditions for algebra functors, including the evolution algebra functor, were studied in [60]. Further generalisations include SS-evolution algebras [91] and evolution coalgebras.

This concludes the survey. We now turn to new observations and open problems.

2 Open questions and conjectures

2.1 New observations

In this section we collect several observations that were obtained while preparing the list of problems. Some of them answer (parts of) questions raised in earlier versions of the list, and they explain the present formulation of several questions below. Throughout, μm​(𝕜)\mu_{m}(\Bbbk) denotes the group of mm-th roots of unity in 𝕜\Bbbk. Several statements were first found, or are additionally supported, by computer experiments; whenever a statement rests only on such experiments we say so explicitly, and it is not claimed as a theorem.

2.1.1 Polynomial identities

Remark 13.

The class of evolution algebras satisfies no polynomial identity other than the consequences of commutativity. Indeed, let pp be a non-zero element of degree at most dd of the free commutative (non-associative) algebra FF on x1,…,xmx_{1},\dots,x_{m}. The quotient F/F>dF/F_{>d} by the span of the monomials of degree greater than dd is a finite-dimensional commutative algebra in which p⁡(x1,…,xm)=p≠0p(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})=p\neq 0. Since every finite-dimensional commutative algebra is an ideal (in particular, a subalgebra) of a finite-dimensional evolution algebra [42], pp is not an identity of the class of evolution algebras. Hence questions about identities are meaningful only for subclasses.

2.1.2 An evolution algebra with orthogonal symmetry

Proposition 14.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and let AnA_{n} be the evolution algebra with natural basis {e1,…,en,u}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n},u\} and

ei2=u(1≤i≤n),u2=u.e_{i}^{2}=u\quad(1\leq i\leq n),\qquad u^{2}=u.

Then AnA_{n} is non-degenerate and not perfect, and Aut⁡(An)\Aut(A_{n}) is the orthogonal group of the symmetric bilinear form b⁡(x,y)=∑ixi​yib(x,y)=\sum_{i}x_{i}y_{i} on V=span⁡{e1,…,en}V=\mathrm{span}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}. If char⁡𝕜≠2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2, then Der⁡(An)≅𝔰​𝔬n​(𝕜)\Der(A_{n})\cong\mathfrak{so}_{n}(\Bbbk). In particular, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and for n≥3n\geq 3, Der⁡(An)\Der(A_{n}) is a non-zero semisimple Lie algebra.

Proof.

For x=v+y​ux=v+yu with v=∑ixi​ei∈Vv=\sum_{i}x_{i}e_{i}\in V and y∈𝕜y\in\Bbbk we have x​ej=xj​uxe_{j}=x_{j}u and x​u=y​uxu=yu; hence Ann⁡(An)=0\Ann(A_{n})=0, while An2=𝕜​uA_{n}^{2}=\Bbbk u. In particular AnA_{n} is non-degenerate and not perfect. The product of v,w∈Vv,w\in V is v​w=b⁡(v,w)​uvw=b(v,w)u.

Let φ∈Aut⁡(An)\varphi\in\Aut(A_{n}). Since An2=𝕜​uA_{n}^{2}=\Bbbk u, we have φ⁡(u)=c​u\varphi(u)=cu and c2​u=φ⁡(u2)=c​uc^{2}u=\varphi(u^{2})=cu, so c=1c=1. The subspace V={x:x​u=0}V=\{x:xu=0\} is therefore φ\varphi-invariant, and for v,w∈Vv,w\in V we get

b⁡(φ​v,φ​w)​u=φ⁡(v)​φ​(w)=φ⁡(v​w)=b⁡(v,w)​ub(\varphi v,\varphi w)u=\varphi(v)\varphi(w)=\varphi(vw)=b(v,w)u.

Conversely every isometry gg of bb, extended by u↦uu\mapsto u, is an automorphism. Thus Aut⁡(An)≅O⁡(V,b)\Aut(A_{n})\cong O(V,b).

Let d∈Der⁡(An)d\in\Der(A_{n}) and char⁡𝕜≠2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2. Write d⁡(u)=c​u+v0d(u)=cu+v_{0} with v0∈Vv_{0}\in V. From u2=uu^{2}=u we get 2​u​d​(u)=d⁡(u)2ud(u)=d(u), that is 2​c​u=c​u+v02cu=cu+v_{0}, so c=0c=0 and v0=0v_{0}=0. Write d⁡(ei)=∑jaj​i​ej+bi​ud(e_{i})=\sum_{j}a_{ji}e_{j}+b_{i}u. From ei​u=0e_{i}u=0 we get d⁡(ei)​u=bi​u=0d(e_{i})u=b_{i}u=0; from ei​ej=0e_{i}e_{j}=0 (i≠ji\neq j) we get aj​i+ai​j=0a_{ji}+a_{ij}=0; and from ei2=ue_{i}^{2}=u we get 2​ai​i​u=d⁡(u)=02a_{ii}u=d(u)=0. Hence dd is a skew-symmetric endomorphism of VV extended by d⁡(u)=0d(u)=0, and every such map is a derivation. ∎

For n=2n=2 the group O⁡(V,b)O(V,b) is infinite over every infinite field, in every characteristic: if char⁡𝕜≠2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2 it contains the rotations (a−cca)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&-c\\ c&a\end{smallmatrix}\right) with a2+c2=1a^{2}+c^{2}=1, a conic with infinitely many rational points, and if char⁡𝕜=2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk=2 it contains the matrices (a1+a1+aa)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&1+a\\ 1+a&a\end{smallmatrix}\right), a∈𝕜a\in\Bbbk.

Remark 15.

The same argument applies to the algebra with ei2=εi​ue_{i}^{2}=\varepsilon_{i}u (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) and u2=uu^{2}=u, where εi∈𝕜×\varepsilon_{i}\in\Bbbk^{\times}: its automorphism group is the orthogonal group of the diagonal form bε​(x,y)=∑iεi​xi​yib_{\varepsilon}(x,y)=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}x_{i}y_{i} and, if char⁡𝕜≠2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2, its derivation algebra is 𝔰​𝔬​(V,bε)\mathfrak{so}(V,b_{\varepsilon}). In particular, over ℝ\mathbb{R} every group O⁡(p,q)O(p,q) (and its Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔬​(p,q)\mathfrak{so}(p,q)) is realised, and in characteristic different from 22 the orthogonal group of every non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form is the automorphism group of a non-degenerate evolution algebra.

2.1.3 The automorphism growth function

For a class 𝒞\mathcal{C} of finite-dimensional evolution algebras let f⁡(X)=|Aut⁡(X)|/dimX∈ℚ>0∪{∞}f(X)=|\Aut(X)|/\dim X\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}. Molinier [87] proved that ff takes every value of ℚ>0\mathbb{Q}_{>0} on perfect evolution algebras.

Theorem 16.

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be an infinite field. Then

  1. (1)

    f⁡(nilpotent evolution algebras)={∞}f(\text{nilpotent evolution algebras})=\{\infty\};

  2. (2)

    f⁡(non-degenerate evolution algebras)=ℚ>0∪{∞}f(\text{non-degenerate evolution algebras})=\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\};

  3. (3)

    f⁡(simple evolution algebras)=ℚ>0f(\text{simple evolution algebras})=\mathbb{Q}_{>0} (this holds over every field, by Corollary 11).

Proof.

(1) Let A≠0A\neq 0 be nilpotent. Then A2≠AA^{2}\neq A and Ann⁡(A)≠0\Ann(A)\neq 0. Choose a non-zero linear form λ\lambda vanishing on A2A^{2}, a non-zero z∈Ann⁡(A)z\in\Ann(A), and put ψ⁡(x)=λ⁡(x)​z\psi(x)=\lambda(x)z. For t∈𝕜t\in\Bbbk the map φt=id+t​ψ\varphi_{t}=\mathrm{id}+t\psi satisfies φt​(x)​φt​(y)=x​y=φt​(x​y)\varphi_{t}(x)\varphi_{t}(y)=xy=\varphi_{t}(xy), because ψ⁡(A)⊆Ann⁡(A)\psi(A)\subseteq\Ann(A) and ψ⁡(A2)=0\psi(A^{2})=0. It is invertible whenever 1+t​λ​(z)≠01+t\lambda(z)\neq 0, which excludes at most one value of tt. Hence Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) is infinite.

(2) Perfect algebras are non-degenerate, so ℚ>0\mathbb{Q}_{>0} is contained in the image by [87]; the value ∞\infty is attained by A2A_{2} of Proposition 14.

(3) The argument below is the one of [45], which works over fields with sufficiently many elements; Corollary 11 gives a different proof valid over every field. Simple algebras are perfect, so their automorphism groups are finite [48]. Let p,qp,q be positive integers and choose NN with s=N2​q2−N⁡(p+q)≥0s=N^{2}q^{2}-N(p+q)\geq 0. Put a=p​Na=pN, b=q​Nb=qN and let G=ℤa×ℤbG=\mathbb{Z}_{a}\times\mathbb{Z}_{b} act on X=ℤa⊔ℤb⊔{1,…,s}X=\mathbb{Z}_{a}\sqcup\mathbb{Z}_{b}\sqcup\{1,\dots,s\}, the first factor by translations on ℤa\mathbb{Z}_{a}, the second by translations on ℤb\mathbb{Z}_{b}, both fixing the remaining points. Then |X|=N2​q2|X|=N^{2}q^{2} and |G|/|X|=p/q|G|/|X|=p/q.

The group GG is 22-closed, i.e. it is the full group of permutations of XX preserving all orbitals of GG (the orbits of GG on X×XX\times X). Indeed, such a permutation σ\sigma preserves each GG-orbit on XX; on ℤa\mathbb{Z}_{a} the orbitals are those of the regular action of ℤa\mathbb{Z}_{a}, so σ⁡(x+g)=σ⁡(x)+g\sigma(x+g)=\sigma(x)+g and σ|ℤa\sigma|_{\mathbb{Z}_{a}} is a translation; similarly on ℤb\mathbb{Z}_{b}; and σ\sigma fixes the fixed points. Thus σ∈G\sigma\in G.

Choose a value cO∈𝕜×c_{O}\in\Bbbk^{\times} for every orbital OO and let AA be the evolution algebra with natural basis {ex}x∈X\{e_{x}\}_{x\in X} and ωx​y=cO⁡(x,y)\omega_{xy}=c_{O(x,y)}. The matrix is GG-invariant, so G≤Aut⁡(A)G\leq\Aut(A) acting by permutations of the basis. Since the identity matrix is GG-invariant, det(ωx​y)\det(\omega_{xy}) is a non-zero polynomial in the cOc_{O}. A monomial map ex↦tx​eσ⁡(x)e_{x}\mapsto t_{x}e_{\sigma(x)} is an automorphism if and only if tx2​ωσ​x,σ​y=ty​ωx​yt_{x}^{2}\,\omega_{\sigma x,\sigma y}=t_{y}\,\omega_{xy} for all x,yx,y. Taking x=yx=y gives tx=ωx​x/ωσ​x,σ​xt_{x}=\omega_{xx}/\omega_{\sigma x,\sigma x}, and substituting, the remaining conditions become identities between Laurent monomials in the variables cOc_{O}. If σ∉G\sigma\notin G, then σ\sigma moves some off-diagonal orbital (by 22-closedness, and because preserving all off-diagonal orbitals forces preservation of the GG-orbits, as |X|≥2|X|\geq 2), so for some x≠yx\neq y the variable cO⁡(σ​x,σ​y)c_{O(\sigma x,\sigma y)} occurs on one side and not on the other; hence the condition is a non-trivial Laurent polynomial equation in the cOc_{O}. As 𝕜\Bbbk is infinite, we may choose the cOc_{O} outside the finitely many hypersurfaces so obtained and outside det=0\det=0. Then AA is perfect, its graph is the complete digraph with loops, so AA is simple [22], the automorphisms of AA (which are monomial [48]) have σ∈G\sigma\in G, and for σ∈G\sigma\in G we get tx=1t_{x}=1 for all xx (the diagonal relations tx2=tyt_{x}^{2}=t_{y} for all x,yx,y force tx=1t_{x}=1). Therefore Aut⁡(A)≅G\Aut(A)\cong G and f⁡(A)=p/qf(A)=p/q. ∎

2.1.4 Idempotents of real perfect evolution algebras

Let AA be perfect with structure matrix MM. By (1), idempotents correspond to solutions of F⁡(x)=Mt​x(2)−x=0F(x)=M^{t}x^{(2)}-x=0, where x(2)=(x12,…,xn2)tx^{(2)}=(x_{1}^{2},\dots,x_{n}^{2})^{t}. Homogenising, a point at infinity would satisfy Mt​x(2)=0M^{t}x^{(2)}=0, i.e. x=0x=0; hence the scheme ZZ of solutions is finite of length 2n2^{n} by Bézout’s theorem, and the origin is a reduced point of ZZ because the Jacobian of FF at 00 is −I-I.

Theorem 17.

Let RR be a real closed field (for instance R=ℝR=\mathbb{R}) and n≥1n\geq 1. The set of cardinalities of the sets of idempotents (including 00) of nn-dimensional perfect evolution RR-algebras is exactly {2,3,…,2n}\{2,3,\dots,2^{n}\}.

Proof.

Upper bound: ZZ has length 2n2^{n}. Lower bound: complex conjugation acts on the R¯\overline{R}-points of Z∖{0}Z\setminus\{0\} preserving multiplicities, and the total multiplicity 2n−12^{n}-1 is odd, so there is a real non-zero idempotent. (This parity argument is a special case of Theorem 18(1) below.)

For the construction we use structure matrices for which the idempotent equations are triangular:

x1=ω1x12,xj=xj2+∑i<jωi​jxi2(2≤j≤n),x_{1}=\omega_{1}x_{1}^{2},\qquad x_{j}=x_{j}^{2}+\sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}x_{i}^{2}\quad(2\leq j\leq n),

with ω1≠0\omega_{1}\neq 0 (the matrix MtM^{t} is lower triangular with non-zero diagonal, so AA is perfect). Let Sj⊆RjS_{j}\subseteq R^{j} be the set of solutions of the first jj equations. We claim that, by suitable choices of ωi​j>0\omega_{ij}>0, the cardinality |Sj||S_{j}| can be made equal to any prescribed integer in [2,2​|Sj−1|][2,2|S_{j-1}|], and that the map s↦s(2)s\mapsto s^{(2)} is injective on SjS_{j}. Clearly |S1|=2|S_{1}|=2 and s↦s(2)s\mapsto s^{(2)} is injective on S1={0,1/ω1}S_{1}=\{0,1/\omega_{1}\}.

Given Sj−1S_{j-1}, put c⁡(s)=∑i<jωi​j​si2c(s)=\sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}s_{i}^{2}; a point s∈Sj−1s\in S_{j-1} has two, one or no extensions to SjS_{j} according as c⁡(s)<1/4c(s)<1/4, c⁡(s)=1/4c(s)=1/4 or c⁡(s)>1/4c(s)>1/4, the extensions being the roots of x2−x+c⁡(s)x^{2}-x+c(s). Two distinct roots r,1−rr,1-r have distinct squares, so injectivity of s↦s(2)s\mapsto s^{(2)} propagates. The points s(2)s^{(2)}, s∈Sj−1s\in S_{j-1}, are distinct and lie in the closed positive orthant, so for a generic choice of positive weights ℓi\ell_{i} the values ℓ⁡(s)=∑iℓi​si2\ell(s)=\sum_{i}\ell_{i}s_{i}^{2} are pairwise distinct, ℓ⁡(0)=0\ell(0)=0 is the smallest one and all others are positive. Let 0=v1<v2<⋯<vN0=v_{1}<v_{2}<\dots<v_{N} be these values. To obtain |Sj|=2​a|S_{j}|=2a (1≤a≤N1\leq a\leq N) choose τ∈(va,va+1)\tau\in(v_{a},v_{a+1}) (or τ>vN\tau>v_{N}), and to obtain |Sj|=2​a+1|S_{j}|=2a+1 (1≤a≤N−11\leq a\leq N-1) choose τ=va+1\tau=v_{a+1}; then put ωi​j=ℓi/(4​τ)\omega_{ij}=\ell_{i}/(4\tau). This realises every integer in [2,2​N][2,2N]. Starting from |Sj−1|=2j−1|S_{j-1}|=2^{j-1} (all intermediate steps chosen maximal) we obtain every value in [2,2n][2,2^{n}] for j=nj=n. ∎

2.1.5 Idempotents over arbitrary fields

Theorem 18.
  1. (1)

    If 𝕜\Bbbk has no finite field extension of odd degree greater than 11, then every perfect finite-dimensional evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra has a non-zero idempotent.

  2. (2)

    Suppose that 𝕜\Bbbk has a field extension L=𝕜⁡(λ)L=\Bbbk(\lambda) of degree 33, where λ3=p​λ2+q​λ+r\lambda^{3}=p\lambda^{2}+q\lambda+r. Then p​q+r≠0pq+r\neq 0, and the two-dimensional evolution algebra

    e12=−q​e1+r​e2p​q+r,e22=e1+p​e2p​q+re_{1}^{2}=\frac{-q\,e_{1}+r\,e_{2}}{pq+r},\qquad e_{2}^{2}=\frac{e_{1}+p\,e_{2}}{pq+r}

    is perfect and has no non-zero idempotent.

  3. (3)

    Consequently, every perfect two-dimensional evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra has a non-zero idempotent if and only if 𝕜\Bbbk has no field extension of degree 33.

Proof.

(1) Let AA be perfect and Z=Spec⁡𝕜⁡[x]/(F)Z=\operatorname{Spec}\Bbbk[x]/(F) as above. Then Z={0}⊔Z′Z=\{0\}\sqcup Z^{\prime}, where {0}\{0\} is a reduced 𝕜\Bbbk-point and Z′Z^{\prime} has length 2n−12^{n}-1. Write Z′Z^{\prime} as a disjoint union of local Artinian schemes with residue fields LiL_{i}; the length of each component is [Li:𝕜][L_{i}:\Bbbk] times its length over LiL_{i}. As 2n−12^{n}-1 is odd, some [Li:𝕜][L_{i}:\Bbbk] is odd, hence Li=𝕜L_{i}=\Bbbk by hypothesis, and Z′Z^{\prime} has a 𝕜\Bbbk-point, i.e. AA has a non-zero idempotent. (This argument works in every characteristic; in characteristic 22 the Jacobian of FF is −I-I everywhere and all points of ZZ are reduced.)

(2) If r=−p​qr=-pq, then λ3−p​λ2−q​λ+p​q=(λ−p)​(λ2−q)\lambda^{3}-p\lambda^{2}-q\lambda+pq=(\lambda-p)(\lambda^{2}-q) would be reducible; hence D=p​q+r≠0D=pq+r\neq 0. The structure matrix has determinant −D/D2≠0-D/D^{2}\neq 0, so the algebra is perfect. The idempotent equations are D​x1=−q​x12+x22Dx_{1}=-qx_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2} and D​x2=r​x12+p​x22Dx_{2}=rx_{1}^{2}+px_{2}^{2}. If x1=0x_{1}=0 then x2=0x_{2}=0. A Gröbner basis computation (easily checked by hand) shows that the ideal generated by the two equations contains x2−x12−p​x1x_{2}-x_{1}^{2}-px_{1} and x1​χ​(x1+p)x_{1}\,\chi(x_{1}+p), where χ⁡(t)=t3−p​t2−q​t−r\chi(t)=t^{3}-pt^{2}-qt-r is the minimal polynomial of λ\lambda. Hence a non-zero idempotent would give a root x1+p∈𝕜x_{1}+p\in\Bbbk of χ\chi, which is impossible.

(3) If 𝕜\Bbbk has a cubic extension, (2) gives a counterexample. Conversely, for n=2n=2 the scheme Z′Z^{\prime} has length 33; if it has no 𝕜\Bbbk-point, then its components have residue degrees in {2,3}\{2,3\} summing (with multiplicities) to 33, which forces a single reduced point with residue field of degree 33. ∎

For example, over ℚ\mathbb{Q} the algebra e12=−e1+e2e_{1}^{2}=-e_{1}+e_{2}, e22=e1e_{2}^{2}=e_{1} (from λ3=λ+1\lambda^{3}=\lambda+1) has no non-zero idempotent; this recovers and explains the failure of the existence of idempotents over ℚ\mathbb{Q} observed in [62]. Since every finite field and every pp-adic field has a cubic extension, perfect evolution algebras without non-zero idempotents exist over all of them in dimension two. Fields satisfying the hypothesis of (1) include algebraically closed fields, real closed fields and, more generally, perfect fields whose absolute Galois group is a pro-22-group. For a “generic” two-dimensional algebra over ℚ\mathbb{Q} the non-zero idempotents are the roots of an irreducible cubic with Galois group S3S_{3}; for instance, for e12=e1+2​e2e_{1}^{2}=e_{1}+2e_{2}, e22=3​e1+5​e2e_{2}^{2}=3e_{1}+5e_{2} the coordinate x1x_{1} of a non-zero idempotent satisfies an irreducible cubic of discriminant −12771-12771.

2.1.6 Diagonal automorphisms

Let AA be perfect with natural basis {ex}\{e_{x}\}. A diagonal map ex↦tx​exe_{x}\mapsto t_{x}e_{x} is an automorphism if and only if ty=tx2t_{y}=t_{x}^{2} for every arrow x→yx\to y of Γ=Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma=\Gamma(A,B). Thus 𝐃⁡(𝕜)={t∈(𝕜×)n:ty=tx2​ for all arrows ​x→y}\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk)=\{t\in(\Bbbk^{\times})^{n}:t_{y}=t_{x}^{2}\text{ for all arrows }x\to y\}.

Remark 19.

Let AA be an nn-dimensional perfect evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra and let A=A1⊕⋯⊕AmA=A_{1}\oplus\dots\oplus A_{m} be its decomposition into indecomposable factors, which are again perfect (Theorem 6). As explained in [50] (see also [1] for the notion of balance),

𝐃⁡(𝕜)≅∏j=1mμ2hj−1​(𝕜),\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk)\cong\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{2^{h_{j}}-1}(\Bbbk),

where hjh_{j} is the balance of the graph of AjA_{j}. Each hjh_{j} is at most dimAj\dim A_{j}, with equality only when AjA_{j} is cyclic (ei2=ei+1e_{i}^{2}=e_{i+1} up to scalars); hence ∑jhj≤n\sum_{j}h_{j}\leq n, and the extreme group μ2n−1​(𝕜)\mu_{2^{n}-1}(\Bbbk) is attained by the indecomposable cyclic algebra of dimension nn. In particular |𝐃⁡(𝕜)||\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk)| is odd, and if 𝕜\Bbbk contains no non-trivial roots of unity of odd order (e.g. 𝕜=ℝ\Bbbk=\mathbb{R} or 𝕜=ℚ\Bbbk=\mathbb{Q}), then 𝐃⁡(𝕜)=1\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk)=1 and Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) embeds into SnS_{n}.

In particular, if char⁡𝕜≠2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2 the group Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) is not abelian, so it is not isomorphic to μ2​(𝕜)×(𝕜,+)\mu_{2}(\Bbbk)\times(\Bbbk,+).

2.1.8 Idempotent-free non-solvable algebras of dimension three

Let W0W_{0} be the two-dimensional commutative algebra with basis v,wv,w and v2=0v^{2}=0, v​w=12​vvw=\frac{1}{2}v, w2=v+ww^{2}=v+w. It is perfect, has no non-zero idempotent (x=α​v+β​wx=\alpha v+\beta w idempotent forces β2=β\beta^{2}=\beta and then β=0\beta=0 by comparing the vv-coefficient), and it is not an evolution algebra (a natural basis would make it a perfect evolution algebra, which has a non-zero idempotent over ℂ\mathbb{C} [58]). For the three-dimensional counterexample E2E_{2} of Hu and Wen [66]

(e12=−e1−e3CLOSE\big(e_{1}^{2}=-e_{1}-e_{3}, e22=−2​e1+2​e2e_{2}^{2}=-2e_{1}+2e_{2}, OPENe32=e1+e3)e_{3}^{2}=e_{1}+e_{3}\big)

one has dimE22=2\dim E_{2}^{2}=2 and E2(∞)=E22≅W0E_{2}^{(\infty)}=E_{2}^{2}\cong W_{0}. The algebra E2E_{2} is isomorphic to the example of [42, Remark 3.9], where it is identified as an evolution envelope of one of the two-dimensional algebras in the classification of Kaygorodov and Volkov [71]. Our computer experiments indicate that the three-dimensional complex evolution algebras with A(∞)=A2≅W0A^{(\infty)}=A^{2}\cong W_{0} form a family with two essential parameters; thus the algebra E2E_{2} is not the only idempotent-free non-solvable evolution algebra in dimension three, and a classification in dimension three is still missing (see Question 9 below). We do not claim this as a theorem.
