b=d=a2b=d=a^{2}, b2=ab^{2}=a, d=c2d=c^{2}, d2=cd^{2}=c, f=ζ​c2f=\zeta c^{2}, e2=f=ζ​be^{2}=f=\zeta b, f2=ef^{2}=e;

these have the solutions a3=1a^{3}=1, b=d=a2b=d=a^{2}, c=ac=a, f=ζ​a2f=\zeta a^{2}, e=ζ2​ae=\zeta^{2}a. Then

φ3​(e1)=a⋅c⋅e​e1=ζ2​a3​e1=ζ2​e1\varphi^{3}(e_{1})=a\cdot c\cdot e\,e_{1}=\zeta^{2}a^{3}e_{1}=\zeta^{2}e_{1},

so φ3\varphi^{3} is a non-trivial diagonal automorphism and φ\varphi has order 99. As

|Aut⁡(A)|=|𝐃⁡(𝕜)|⋅3=9|\Aut(A)|=|\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk)|\cdot 3=9, Aut⁡(A)=⟨φ⟩≅ℤ9\Aut(A)=\langle\varphi\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}_{9}.

∎

2.1.10 Further remarks

Remark 22.

Strong connectivity of Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B), and hence the condensation of the graph, is not independent of the natural basis for non-degenerate algebras. If char⁡𝕜≠2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2 and e12=e22=e1+e2e_{1}^{2}=e_{2}^{2}=e_{1}+e_{2}, then Γ⁡(A,{e1,e2})\Gamma(A,\{e_{1},e_{2}\}) is the complete digraph with loops, while f=e1−e2f=e_{1}-e_{2}, g=e1+e2g=e_{1}+e_{2} is a natural basis with f2=g2=2​gf^{2}=g^{2}=2g, whose graph is not strongly connected.

Remark 23.

Let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be a finite field. The average number of non-zero idempotents of a perfect evolution algebra with a uniformly random invertible structure matrix is exactly 11. Indeed, for fixed x≠0x\neq 0 we have x(2)≠0x^{(2)}\neq 0, and the number of N∈GLn⁡(𝔽q)N\in\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) with N​x(2)=xNx^{(2)}=x is |GLn⁡(𝔽q)|/(qn−1)|\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})|/(q^{n}-1); summing over the qn−1q^{n}-1 non-zero vectors xx gives |GLn⁡(𝔽q)||\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})| pairs.

2.1.11 Formal verification

The following statements of this section have been formalised and proved in the proof assistant Lean 4 with the Mathlib library (the proofs contain no unproved steps and use only the standard axioms). An evolution algebra is encoded by its structure matrix ω=(ωi​j)\omega=(\omega_{ij}) acting on 𝕜n\Bbbk^{n}, with product (x​y)j=∑iωi​j​xi​yi(xy)_{j}=\sum_{i}\omega_{ij}x_{i}y_{i}; perfect means detω≠0\det\omega\neq 0.

  • •

    Proposition 14 in full: AnA_{n} is non-degenerate and not perfect, an invertible linear map is an automorphism of AnA_{n} if and only if it is an orthogonal matrix extended by u↦uu\mapsto u, the derivations are exactly the skew-symmetric matrices extended by u↦0u\mapsto 0, and O2​(𝕜)O_{2}(\Bbbk), hence Aut⁡(A2)\Aut(A_{2}), is infinite over every infinite field.

  • •

    Theorem 16(1) (in the slightly more general form: A2≠AA^{2}\neq A and Ann⁡(A)≠0\Ann(A)\neq 0 imply |Aut⁡(A)|=∞|\Aut(A)|=\infty over an infinite field), and the value ∞\infty in (2). The values in ℚ>0\mathbb{Q}_{>0} in (2) rest on [87], and part (3) was not formalised.

  • •

    Theorem 17 in full. The upper bound 2n2^{n} is proved for every field, by showing that the coordinate ring of the scheme of idempotents of a perfect algebra has dimension exactly 2n2^{n}.

  • •

    Theorem 18 in full, in fact with the weaker hypothesis in (1) that 𝕜\Bbbk has no field extension of odd degree dd with 1<d≤2n−11<d\leq 2^{n}-1; also the example over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, the existence of idempotent-free perfect two-dimensional algebras over every finite field, and the irreducibility and the discriminant −12771-12771 of the cubic in the generic example.

  • •

    Remark 19 in part: 𝐃⁡(𝕜)\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk) is finite of odd order, it is trivial if 𝕜\Bbbk has no non-trivial roots of unity of odd order, and in that case Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) embeds into SnS_{n} (automorphisms of perfect algebras are monomial). The product decomposition was not formalised.

  • •

    The description of Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) in Proposition 20(3): every automorphism is one of the maps φs,c\varphi_{s,c} with s2=1s^{2}=1, all of them are automorphisms, they are pairwise distinct, and φs,c​φs′,c′=φs​s′,s′​c+c′\varphi_{s,c}\varphi_{s^{\prime},c^{\prime}}=\varphi_{ss^{\prime},\,s^{\prime}c+c^{\prime}}. Moreover, for every strictly upper triangular structure matrix of size at least 22 the maps φs,c\varphi_{s,c} are automorphisms and Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) is not abelian if char⁡𝕜≠2\operatorname{char}\Bbbk\neq 2; in particular Aut⁡(A)≇μ2​(𝕜)×(𝕜,+)\Aut(A)\not\cong\mu_{2}(\Bbbk)\times(\Bbbk,+). The statement on Der⁡(A)\Der(A) was not formalised.

  • •

    Proposition 21 in full: the algebra is perfect and Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) is cyclic of order 99.

  • •

    Remarks 22 and 23; the latter in the form ∑ω∈GLn⁡(𝔽q)#⁡{x≠0:x2=x}=|GLn⁡(𝔽q)|\sum_{\omega\in\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})}\#\{x\neq 0:x^{2}=x\}=|\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})| for n≥1n\geq 1, where x2x^{2} is computed with the structure matrix ω\omega.

  • •

    Theorem 10 except the simplicity statement: for every field 𝕜\Bbbk and every finite loopless digraph Δ\Delta, the structure matrix of AΔA_{\Delta} is invertible over 𝕜\Bbbk, and Aut⁡(AΔ)≅Aut⁡(Δ)\Aut(A_{\Delta})\cong\Aut(\Delta) as groups.

Remark 13, parts (1), (2) and the dimension count of Proposition 20, and the experimental statements were not formalised. The simplicity statement of Theorem 10 (which follows from Theorem 6), Corollary 11, Proposition 9 and Remarks 15, 12 were not formalised.

2.2 Open questions

The following list merges and revises the two lists of problems in an earlier version of this text (nine problems proposed by the authors and colleagues, and thirty further problems motivated by the literature), and adds new questions. Questions which were (partly) answered by the observations of Section 2.1 have been reformulated accordingly. After each question we indicate its source and what is known.

2.2.1 Foundations

Question 1 (Non-cancellation).

Let AA be a non-degenerate finite-dimensional evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra. Is it true that there exist non-degenerate finite-dimensional evolution algebras B≇CB\not\cong C with A⊗B≅A⊗CA\otimes B\cong A\otimes C if and only if each indecomposable direct summand of AA has balance greater than 11? Equivalently, is [A][A] a zero-divisor of the Grothendieck ring of non-degenerate evolution algebras exactly in this case?

Source and status: [1, Conjecture 1.1]; one implication and the case of direct sums of cyclic algebras are proved in [1]. Proposed by I. Alshatnawi, C. Costoya and A. Viruel.

Question 2 (The category of evolution algebras).

The full subcategory 𝖤𝗏𝗈𝕜\mathsf{Evo}_{\Bbbk} of 𝕜\Bbbk-algebras spanned by evolution algebras is not complete, and subalgebras of evolution algebras need not be evolution algebras. Is there a categorical framework for evolution algebras (for instance, objects equipped with a natural basis or a family of natural bases, with suitable morphisms) with good limits, colimits and functorial constructions?

Source and status: Proposed by J. M. Moreno Fernández and A. Viruel.

Question 3 (Homological algebra).

Develop a (co)homology theory of evolution algebras governing extensions of evolution algebras by evolution algebras and formal deformations inside the class of evolution algebras.

Source and status: Proposed by A. Viruel; deformations are considered in [83].

Question 4 (Evolution algebras over rings).

Find a definition of evolution algebras over a commutative ring RR that does not require the underlying module to be free. Do the reductions E/𝔪​EE/\mathfrak{m}E at maximal ideals determine EE? Is there a notion of perfection over RR with a uniqueness theorem for natural bases generalising the one over fields, and a well-behaved category of such algebras?

Source and status: Proposed by D. Martín Barquero and C. Martín González; rank two over domains is treated in [16].

Question 5 (Tensor products and factorisation).

Characterise in terms of the factors when A⊗BA\otimes B is simple, perfect, non-degenerate or indecomposable, and describe the role of the periods of the graphs. Does every non-degenerate evolution algebra factor into tensor-indecomposable ones, and to what extent is the factorisation unique?

Source and status: [17, 1]. The question is partially answered in [1, Section 5] in terms of the balance.

Question 6 (The Grothendieck ring).

Find generators and relations, the Krull dimension and the nilradical of the Grothendieck ring of non-degenerate evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebras, decide whether it is Noetherian, and describe all its zero-divisors and its dependence on 𝕜\Bbbk.

Source and status: [1].

2.2.2 Structure theory

Question 7 (Intrinsic characterisation of solvability).

Find a graph-theoretic or matrix-theoretic characterisation of solvable finite-dimensional evolution algebras, analogous to the characterisation of nilpotency by the absence of oriented cycles.

Source and status: Motivated by the García-Martínez–Pérez-Rodríguez conjecture [58] and its refutation [66]; a counterexample to the conjecture also appears in [42, Remark 3.9].

Question 8 (Stable term of the derived series).

For which finite-dimensional evolution algebras is A(∞)A^{(\infty)} again an evolution algebra?

Source and status: [66, Question 2.11]; when this holds, absence of idempotents is equivalent to solvability over ℂ\mathbb{C} [66].

Question 9 (Idempotent-free non-solvable algebras).

Classify the idempotent-free non-solvable evolution algebras of dimension 33 and 44 over ℂ\mathbb{C}. In dimension 33, is A(∞)A^{(\infty)} always isomorphic to the algebra W0W_{0} of Section 2.1, and do these algebras form a two-parameter family?

Source and status: [66]; see Section 2.1 for computer evidence that the example of [66] is not unique.

Question 10 (Idempotents of non-perfect algebras).

Give a criterion, in terms of the structure matrix or the graphs, for a (not necessarily perfect) finite-dimensional complex evolution algebra to have a non-zero idempotent.

Source and status: Described as open in [58].

Question 11 (Idempotents over arbitrary fields).

For n≥3n\geq 3, characterise the fields 𝕜\Bbbk over which every perfect nn-dimensional evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra has a non-zero idempotent. Does the class of such fields depend on nn?

Source and status: Theorem 18 settles n=2n=2 and gives a sufficient condition for all nn; see also Conjecture 1.

Question 12 (Hereditary evolution algebras).

Characterise the evolution algebras all of whose subalgebras are evolution algebras. Is this property detected by the graphs? Is it preserved by tensor products and direct sums? What about ideals?

Source and status: [32, 58, 77].

Question 13 (Subalgebra lattices).

Characterise modular, distributive and dually atomistic evolution algebras in general. If two evolution algebras have isomorphic subalgebra lattices, how are they related? Characterise the evolution algebras whose Frattini subalgebra is an ideal, and the Frattini-free ones.

Source and status: [75, 78, 76].

Question 14 (Natural bases of non-perfect algebras).

Describe the set of natural bases (up to permutation and scaling) of a non-degenerate evolution algebra. When is it finite? Can it be infinite for an algebra whose automorphism group is finite?

Source and status: New. Proposition 14 shows that the set can be infinite (it contains all orthogonal bases of VV completed by uu) even for a non-degenerate algebra; Remark 22 shows that the graphs of different natural bases can differ in strong connectivity. [5, Corollary 2.13] describes all the natural bases of an evolution algebra (degenerate or not) in terms of its decomposition into natural ideals; it does not give a formula for the number of natural bases, but comes close to it.

Question 15 (Nil versus nilpotent).

Give a combinatorial characterisation of nil evolution algebras of arbitrary dimension in terms of Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B). Is a finitely generated evolution algebra which is nil of bounded index (with respect to principal powers) necessarily nilpotent?

Source and status: [114, 28]. With respect to plenary powers the answer is negative, already in finite dimension (Proposition 9); with respect to principal powers, finite-dimensional nil evolution algebras are nilpotent (Theorem 5).

Question 16 (Identities of subclasses).

By Remark 13, evolution algebras satisfy only the consequences of commutativity. Describe the identities of natural subclasses: the algebras EnE_{n} of [29], algebras with dimA2≤r\dim A^{2}\leq r, nilpotent algebras of index at most mm, algebras whose graphs have bounded out-degree. Are the corresponding T-ideals finitely generated, and are the varieties generated by a single finite-dimensional algebra?

Source and status: [29, 42].

Question 17 (Radicals and combinatorial detectability).

Which algebraic properties of a non-perfect evolution algebra (semiprimeness, primeness, regularity, existence of non-trivial radicals) can be read off from a single natural basis, which from the family of all graphs, and which from neither?

Source and status: [9, 24, 20]; semiprimeness and perfection are not combinatorial [9].

2.2.3 Classification, moduli and geometry

Question 18 (The variety of evolution algebras).

The closure of the set 𝖤𝗏𝗈n\mathsf{Evo}_{n} of evolution algebra structures in the variety of commutative algebras on 𝕜n\Bbbk^{n} is irreducible of dimension 2​n2−n2n^{2}-n. Find its equations, describe the algebras in 𝖤𝗏𝗈n¯∖𝖤𝗏𝗈n\overline{\mathsf{Evo}_{n}}\setminus\mathsf{Evo}_{n}, and relate them to the simultaneous diagonalisation by congruence problem.

Source and status: [6].

Question 19 (Degenerations and rigidity).

Determine the rigid evolution algebras and the degeneration diagrams of (nilpotent) evolution algebras in dimension at least 55. Is the generic nilpotent evolution algebra of Proposition 20 rigid within 𝒩n\mathcal{N}_{n} when n=4n=4?

Source and status: [83]; irreducibility and dimension of 𝒩n\mathcal{N}_{n} are in Proposition 20.

Question 20 (Nilpotent algebras of dimension six).

Classify six-dimensional nilpotent evolution algebras over algebraically closed fields. By Proposition 20 the generic family depends on five parameters.

Source and status: New; dimension five is treated in [65, 49].

Question 21 (Counting asymptotics).

Determine the asymptotic number of isomorphism classes of all (not necessarily perfect) nn-dimensional evolution 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebras as n→∞n\to\infty.

Source and status: [119]; see also Conjecture 8.

Question 22 (Random evolution algebras).

For random structure matrices (uniform over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, Gaussian over ℝ\mathbb{R}, supported on a random digraph), what are the asymptotic probabilities of being simple, indecomposable, having trivial automorphism group, or having exactly kk real non-zero idempotents? Are there sharp thresholds in the sparse regime?

Source and status: [1, 119]; the expected number of non-zero idempotents over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} is 11 (Remark 23).

Question 23 (Isotopy).

Classify four-dimensional evolution algebras up to isotopy over arbitrary fields.

Source and status: Dimensions two and three are treated in [51, 52].

Question 24 (Autotopy group schemes).

Describe the autotopy group scheme of a perfect evolution algebra by an exact sequence analogous to (2) with terms depending only on the graph, and relate it to the group scheme of ternary automorphisms.

Source and status: [85], [38, Problem 4.1].

Question 25 (Simple evolution algebras).

Classify four-dimensional simple evolution algebras over arbitrary fields.

Source and status: [18], [111], [38, Problem 3.2]. The two other parts of an earlier formulation have been removed, since they have immediate answers. If Γ=Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma=\Gamma(A,B) is strongly connected, its period dd is the greatest common divisor of the lengths of its oriented cycles; the vertices then split into classes C0,…,Cd−1C_{0},\dots,C_{d-1} such that every arrow goes from some CiC_{i} to Ci+1C_{i+1} (indices modulo dd), and A=⨁iAiA=\bigoplus_{i}A_{i} with Ai=span⁡{ex:x∈Ci}A_{i}=\mathrm{span}\{e_{x}:x\in C_{i}\} satisfies Ai2⊆Ai+1A_{i}^{2}\subseteq A_{i+1} and Ai​Aj=0A_{i}A_{j}=0 for i≠ji\neq j, over every field (this is Tian’s periodic decomposition [111]). Moreover, by Theorem 6 a simple evolution algebra is perfect with strongly connected graph, and both properties are preserved by extension of scalars; hence every simple finite-dimensional evolution algebra is absolutely simple.

2.2.4 Graphs, combinatorics and spectra

Question 26 (Graphs versus random walks).

Prove that for every finite connected graph GG one has A⁡(G)≅AR​W​(G)A(G)\cong A_{RW}(G) if and only if GG is regular or biregular.

Source and status: Known for non-singular graphs [25, 26]; supporting families in [27].

Question 27 (Basis-independent graph invariants).

Determine the graph-theoretic invariants of Γ⁡(A,B)\Gamma(A,B) that do not depend on BB for non-degenerate evolution algebras. Is there a complete system of such invariants in some natural class? Is the balance independent of the natural basis for arbitrary (possibly degenerate) evolution algebras?

Source and status: Balance is invariant for non-degenerate algebras [1]; for degenerate algebras this is not known; strong connectivity and the condensation are not (Remark 22); see also [59, Open Problem 3].

Question 28 (Spectral theory).

Find spectral invariants of evolution algebras independent of the natural basis, and relate them to expansion and to Tian’s hierarchy. Characterise algebraically the expander and Ramanujan evolution algebras over finite fields.

Source and status: [38, Problem 3.1], [59, Open Problem 1].

Question 29 (Universality).

Is the category of (perfect) evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebras algebraically universal in the sense of Pultr and Trnková? Is there at least a full embedding of the category of graphs into it?

Source and status: [43, 99].

Question 30 (Simultaneous graphical realisation).

Given digraphs G1,…,GmG_{1},\dots,G_{m} on dd vertices, decide whether there are a dd-dimensional evolution algebra AA and natural bases BiB_{i} with Γ⁡(A,Bi)≅Gi\Gamma(A,B_{i})\cong G_{i}, and describe the class of such algebras.

Source and status: Proposed by A. Viruel. If Gi≇GjG_{i}\not\cong G_{j} for some i,ji,j, such algebras are not perfect.

2.2.5 Automorphisms, derivations and operators

Question 31 (Realisation of algebraic groups).

Let GG be a linear algebraic group over 𝕜\Bbbk. Is there a finite-dimensional evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra AA with Aut⁡(A)≅G⁡(𝕜)\Aut(A)\cong G(\Bbbk) as abstract groups? with Aut⁡(A)≅G\Aut(A)\cong G as algebraic groups? with 𝐀𝐮𝐭⁡(A)≅G\mathbf{Aut}(A)\cong G as group schemes?

Source and status: Proposed by C. Costoya and A. Viruel. Finite groups are realised [43, 109]; without the evolution condition the answer is positive [63]; OnO_{n} and GLn\GL_{n} are realised (Proposition 14 and the zero algebra), and so are the orthogonal groups of all diagonal non-degenerate forms, e.g. O⁡(p,q)O(p,q) over ℝ\mathbb{R} (Remark 15).

Question 32 (Permutation representations).

Characterise the permutation representations ξ:G→Sn\xi\colon G\to S_{n} for which there is a perfect nn-dimensional evolution algebra XX with Aut⁡(X)≅G\Aut(X)\cong G and ρX\rho_{X} equivalent to ξ\xi.

Source and status: Proposed by C. Costoya, P. Mayorga and A. Viruel; partial results in [44].

Question 33 (Extensions in the Elduque–Labra sequence).

Characterise the perfect evolution algebras for which 1→𝐃⁡(𝕜)→Aut⁡(A)→ρ⁡(Aut⁡(A))→11\to\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk)\to\Aut(A)\to\rho(\Aut(A))\to 1 splits. Which extensions of a permutation group by a group of the form ∏μ2hj−1​(𝕜)\prod\mu_{2^{h_{j}}-1}(\Bbbk) occur?

Source and status: New; for the description of 𝐃⁡(𝕜)\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk) see [50] and Remark 19; the new example of Proposition 21 gives a non-split extension.

Question 34 (Growth function over finite fields).

Describe the image of f⁡(X)=|Aut⁡(X)|/dimXf(X)=|\Aut(X)|/\dim X on perfect, nilpotent and non-degenerate evolution algebras over a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Source and status: Proposed by A. Viruel; over infinite fields the answer is given in Theorem 16; on simple algebras the image is ℚ>0\mathbb{Q}_{>0} over every field (Corollary 11).

Question 35 (Ind-schemes).

Develop a theory of automorphism group ind-schemes of infinite-dimensional evolution algebras, extending the description of diagonal automorphism groups as inverse limits (and solenoids).

Source and status: Proposed by D. Martín Barquero and C. Martín González; [10].

Question 36 (Realisation of derivation algebras).

Which finite-dimensional Lie algebras are isomorphic to Der⁡(A)\Der(A) for an evolution algebra AA? Can every nilpotent or solvable Lie algebra be realised? Which semisimple ones?

Source and status: [50, 11, 12]; 𝔰​𝔬n\mathfrak{so}_{n} is realised (Proposition 14); see Conjecture 5.

Question 37 (Smoothness).

For non-perfect evolution algebras, determine when 𝐀𝐮𝐭⁡(A)\mathbf{Aut}(A) is smooth, describe its identity component, and decide when it is generated by exp⁡(Der⁡(A))\exp(\Der(A)).

Source and status: [50, 90].

Question 38 (Hopf algebras and representations).

For perfect evolution algebras of arbitrary dimension, is a faithful tight pp-algebra isomorphic to the Hopf algebra representing 𝐀𝐮𝐭⁡(A)\mathbf{Aut}(A)? Is Aut⁡(A)=1\Aut(A)=1 equivalent to the non-existence of faithful associative commutative representations?

Source and status: Known in dimension two [8].

Question 39 (Rota–Baxter and local maps).

Classify Rota–Baxter operators of arbitrary weight on perfect evolution algebras in terms of the graph and describe the variety of such operators. For which evolution algebras are all local (resp. 22-local) derivations derivations, and all local automorphisms automorphisms?

Source and status: [101, 102, 89].

Question 40 (Minimal dimension).

For a finite group GG and a field 𝕜\Bbbk let μ𝕜​(G)\mu_{\Bbbk}(G) be the minimal dimension of an evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra with automorphism group GG. Estimate μ𝕜​(G)\mu_{\Bbbk}(G) and compare it with the minimal number of vertices of a graph with automorphism group GG.

Source and status: [43, 109]. By Remark 19, for 𝕜=ℂ\Bbbk=\mathbb{C} and G=ℤ3G=\mathbb{Z}_{3} no perfect algebra of dimension at most 22 has automorphism group GG: in dimension at most 22 the group 𝐃⁡(𝕜)\mathbf{D}(\Bbbk) is non-trivial only when the graph is a 22-cycle, and then |Aut⁡(A)|=6|\Aut(A)|=6; otherwise Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A) embeds into S2S_{2}. Using the Cayley evolution algebras of [45], μ𝕜​(G)≤|G|\mu_{\Bbbk}(G)\leq|G| for every infinite field 𝕜\Bbbk. By Theorem 10, μ𝕜​(G)≤2​m\mu_{\Bbbk}(G)\leq 2m for every field 𝕜\Bbbk, where mm is the minimal number of vertices of a strongly connected digraph (for instance, of a connected graph) with automorphism group GG.

Question 41 (Small fields; answered).

Source and status: Answered: over every field every finite group is the automorphism group of a simple evolution algebra (Theorem 10), and simple evolution algebras are automatically absolutely simple (see the comments after Question 25).

2.2.6 Embeddings and generalisations

Question 42 (Evolution envelopes).

Is the upper bound n⁡(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2 for the minimal dimension of an evolution algebra containing a given nn-dimensional commutative algebra as an ideal attained? Which commutative algebras have a unique minimal evolution envelope? Does the embedding theorem extend to infinite-dimensional commutative algebras?

Source and status: [42, Questions 3.7, 5.8, 2.3].

Question 43 (mm-ary evolution algebras).

Does every finite-dimensional commutative mm-ary algebra embed into an mm-ary evolution algebra? Which results on graphs, automorphism group schemes and universality extend?

Source and status: [42, Question 4.7].

2.2.7 Arithmetic

Question 44 (Forms).

Compute H1​(𝕜,𝐀𝐮𝐭​(A))H^{1}(\Bbbk,\mathbf{Aut}(A)) for perfect AA in terms of the graph and the groups 𝕜×/(𝕜×)N\Bbbk^{\times}/(\Bbbk^{\times})^{N}. Which twisted forms of a perfect evolution algebra are again evolution algebras?

Source and status: [50]. A quadratic field extension is a form of 𝕜×𝕜\Bbbk\times\Bbbk without natural basis. See Conjecture 7 for the Hasse principle.

Question 45 (Reduction modulo primes).

For a perfect evolution ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra, describe the primes pp for which a ℤ(p)\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}-model reduces to a perfect evolution 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-algebra with the same graph, and compare the automorphism groups and idempotents before and after reduction.

Source and status: New; compare Question 4.

2.2.8 Infinite dimension, probability and dynamics

Question 46 (Hilbert evolution algebras).

If the square of a Hilbert evolution algebra is dense, is its natural orthonormal basis unique up to permutation and unimodular scalars? Describe bounded derivations and automorphisms, and the spectral theory of the evolution operator.

Source and status: [118, 28].

Question 47 (Markov chains and Gibbs measures).

Characterise recurrence, transience and positive recurrence of countable Markov chains by algebraic properties of the associated evolution algebras. Does a phase transition correspond to an algebraic property of the algebras of [41]?

Source and status: [118, 41].

Question 48 (Dynamics of the evolution operator).

Characterise, in terms of the structure matrix and the graph, the non-negative real evolution algebras for which all trajectories of x↦x2x\mapsto x^{2} (or its normalisation) converge, and the existence and stability of periodic orbits.

Source and status: [111, 107].

Question 49 (Chains and flows).

Classify chains of evolution algebras up to time-dependent isomorphism, characterise the chains whose isomorphism type is eventually constant, and describe the evolution of idempotents, nilpotency and simplicity along chains and flows.

Source and status: [34, 88].

2.2.9 Algorithms

Question 50 (Algorithms and complexity).

What is the complexity of deciding whether an algebra over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is an evolution algebra and of computing all its natural bases? What is the complexity of the isomorphism problem for perfect evolution algebras over finite fields relative to graph isomorphism? Can low-dimensional classifications be certified by computer, for instance in a proof assistant?

Source and status: [6, 43]. By [42], over a field of characteristic different from 22, deciding whether an algebra is an evolution algebra is equivalent to computing a Waring decomposition of the quadratic map x↦x2x\mapsto x^{2} given by the product; in general this is an NP-hard problem, see [108].

2.3 Conjectures

Each conjecture below is accompanied by the evidence we have. For each of them a direct attempt to prove or disprove it (of the order of half an hour of focused work, including the natural first ideas indicated in the comments) did not succeed; in particular none of them follows in an obvious way from the results surveyed in Section 1 or from the observations of Section 2.1. Computer evidence was obtained with short scripts (exact arithmetic over finite fields, or numerical computation); it is experimental and is not a proof.

Conjecture 1 (Fields with odd-degree extensions).

If 𝕜\Bbbk has a finite separable extension of odd degree greater than 11, then for some nn there is a perfect nn-dimensional evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra without non-zero idempotents. Together with Theorem 18(1) this would characterise the fields over which every perfect evolution algebra has a non-zero idempotent.

Source and status: Proved when 𝕜\Bbbk has a cubic extension (Theorem 18(2)). The natural idea of realising a given odd-degree extension L/𝕜L/\Bbbk as the residue field of the scheme Z′Z^{\prime} of non-zero idempotents requires controlling all 2n−12^{n}-1 points simultaneously, and we could not do this already for extensions of degree 55 without cubic subextensions.

Conjecture 2 (Generic Galois group of idempotents).

For the generic nn-dimensional evolution algebra over ℚ\mathbb{Q} (structure constants independent indeterminates), the Galois group of the 2n−12^{n}-1 non-zero idempotents is the full symmetric group S2n−1S_{2^{n}-1}. Consequently, by Chebotarev’s theorem, for fixed nn and q→∞q\to\infty the number of non-zero idempotents of a random perfect evolution 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebra is distributed like the number of fixed points of a random permutation of 2n−12^{n}-1 letters; in particular the probability of having no non-zero idempotent tends to ∑k=02n−1(−1)k/k!\sum_{k=0}^{2^{n}-1}(-1)^{k}/k!.

Source and status: Proved for n=2n=2 (the example after Theorem 18 specialises the generic cubic to one with Galois group S3S_{3}). The mean value 11 agrees with Remark 23 for every qq. Computer experiments with random matrices over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} for n=2n=2 (p=101,211p=101,211) and n=3n=3 (p=31,53p=31,53) give distributions of the number of non-zero idempotents close to the fixed-point distribution of S3S_{3} and S7S_{7}. Showing that the monodromy group is 22-transitive and contains a transposition seems to require a degeneration argument that we could not complete for n=3n=3.

Conjecture 3 (Largest automorphism groups of perfect algebras).

Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, the maximal order of the automorphism group of a perfect nn-dimensional evolution algebra is

max⁡{∏l(l⁡(2l−1))ml​ml!:∑ll​ml=n},\max\Bigl\{\prod_{l}\bigl(l(2^{l}-1)\bigr)^{m_{l}}m_{l}!\;:\;\sum_{l}lm_{l}=n\Bigr\},

that is 1,6,21,72,155,12961,6,21,72,155,1296 for n=1,…,6n=1,\dots,6 and n!n! for n≥7n\geq 7.

Source and status: The values are attained by direct sums of cyclic algebras ei2=ei+1e_{i}^{2}=e_{i+1} (the automorphism group of a direct sum of mm copies of a perfect indecomposable algebra CC is Aut⁡(C)≀Sm\Aut(C)\wr S_{m}). The upper bound was checked for n≤4n\leq 4 by a computer enumeration using the bound |Aut⁡(A)|≤|𝐃⁡(ℂ)|⋅|Aut⁡(Γ)||\Aut(A)|\leq|\mathbf{D}(\mathbb{C})|\cdot|\Aut(\Gamma)| over all digraphs Γ\Gamma that are graphs of perfect algebras. Remark 19 bounds |𝐃||\mathbf{D}| but the interplay between 𝐃\mathbf{D} and the permutation part is what we could not control in general.

Conjecture 4 (Largest automorphism groups of simple algebras).

Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, the maximal order of the automorphism group of a simple nn-dimensional evolution algebra is max⁡{n!,n⁡(2n−1)}\max\{n!,\;n(2^{n}-1)\}.

Source and status: Both values are attained: n⁡(2n−1)n(2^{n}-1) by the cyclic algebra ei2=ei+1e_{i}^{2}=e_{i+1}, and n!n! by ei2=a​ei+b​∑j≠ieje_{i}^{2}=ae_{i}+b\sum_{j\neq i}e_{j} for generic a,ba,b (complete graph with loops, so 𝐃=1\mathbf{D}=1). Verified for n≤4n\leq 4 by the same computer enumeration as in Conjecture 3. The complex nn-dimensional evolution algebras with automorphism group SnS_{n} are classified in [109].

Conjecture 5 (Semisimple derivation algebras).

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be algebraically closed of characteristic 00. If Der⁡(A)\Der(A) is semisimple for a finite-dimensional evolution algebra AA, then Der⁡(A)≅⨁i𝔰​𝔬mi\Der(A)\cong\bigoplus_{i}\mathfrak{so}_{m_{i}} with mi≥3m_{i}\geq 3.

Source and status: Proposition 14 realises 𝔰​𝔬m\mathfrak{so}_{m}. Heuristically, derivations of an algebra with a natural basis must preserve a family of quadratic forms simultaneously diagonalised by that basis, and the orthogonal algebras are the natural semisimple symmetry algebras of such configurations. We know no example in which a simple Lie algebra not isomorphic to some 𝔰​𝔬m\mathfrak{so}_{m} (for instance 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3} or 𝔤2\mathfrak{g}_{2}) occurs as an ideal of a derivation algebra, but we could not exclude, for instance, 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3} acting on a non-degenerate algebra whose square has dimension greater than one.

Conjecture 6 (Numbers of complex idempotents).

For every nn and every m∈{2,…,2n}m\in\{2,\dots,2^{n}\} there is a perfect nn-dimensional complex evolution algebra with exactly mm distinct idempotents (including 00). In particular, for every nn there is a perfect complex evolution algebra with a unique non-zero idempotent.

Source and status: True for n≤2n\leq 2: e12=34​e1+14​e2e_{1}^{2}=\frac{3}{4}e_{1}+\frac{1}{4}e_{2}, e22=14​e1+34​e2e_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}e_{1}+\frac{3}{4}e_{2} has the unique non-zero idempotent e1+e2e_{1}+e_{2} (of multiplicity 33), and triangular algebras as in the proof of Theorem 17 give 33 and 44. Over ℝ\mathbb{R} the analogous statement is Theorem 17, but there non-real solutions may be ignored. Triangular constructions only give values ≥n+1\geq n+1, and the symmetric families we tried for n=3n=3 (with S3S_{3}-symmetry) did not produce a unique non-zero idempotent.

Conjecture 7 (Failure of the Hasse principle).

There exist perfect evolution ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebras A,BA,B which are isomorphic over ℝ\mathbb{R} and over ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p} for every prime pp, but not over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Source and status: Forms of a perfect algebra with the same graph are governed by H1​(ℚ,𝐀𝐮𝐭​(A))H^{1}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbf{Aut}(A)). For two-dimensional cyclic algebras the relevant set is ℚ×/(ℚ×)3\mathbb{Q}^{\times}/(\mathbb{Q}^{\times})^{3} (up to the action of the permutation part), and the Hasse principle holds there; failures should come from non-abelian or non-cyclic diagonal parts, where Tate–Shafarevich sets of finite group schemes are known to be non-trivial in general. We could not yet produce an explicit pair.

Conjecture 8 (PORC counting).

For every nn, the number Nn​(q)N_{n}(q) of isomorphism classes of perfect nn-dimensional evolution 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}-algebras is a PORC function of qq (a polynomial on each residue class of qq modulo some integer).

Source and status: The count is given by Burnside’s lemma for Sn⋉(𝔽q×)nS_{n}\ltimes(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{\times})^{n} acting on GLn⁡(𝔽q)\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}), and each fixed-point set is defined by monomial conditions; the difficulty is to show that the number of invertible matrices in each such set is PORC. Computer counts: N2(q)=q2+2​q−12+[q≡1mod3]N_{2}(q)=\frac{q^{2}+2q-1}{2}+[\,q\equiv 1\bmod 3\,] for all odd primes 3≤q≤233\leq q\leq 23, and N3​(3)=249N_{3}(3)=249, N3​(5)=3943N_{3}(5)=3943, N3​(7)=26249N_{3}(7)=26249. Explicit formulas for n≤4n\leq 4 are given in [119].

Conjecture 9 (Spectrum of nilpotency indices).

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be an infinite field. An nn-dimensional nilpotent evolution 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra of nilpotency index k+1k+1 exists if and only if either k=2ak=2^{a} with 0≤a≤n−10\leq a\leq n-1, or kk has at least two non-zero binary digits and ⌊log2⁡k⌋+s2​(k)≤n−1\lfloor\log_{2}k\rfloor+s_{2}(k)\leq n-1, where s2​(k)s_{2}(k) is the number of non-zero binary digits of kk.

Source and status: The case of maximal index 2n−1+12^{n-1}+1 is known [30, 35]. The predicted sets of indices are {2,3,5}\{2,3,5\}, {2,3,4,5,9}\{2,3,4,5,9\}, {2,…,7,9,17}\{2,\dots,7,9,17\} and {2,…,11,13,17,33}\{2,\dots,11,13,17,33\} for n=3,4,5,6n=3,4,5,6. In computer experiments (exact computation modulo a large prime with structure matrices having small integer entries; exhaustive over a fixed set of entries for n≤5n\leq 5 and random for n=6n=6) exactly these indices were found. The lower series of an evolution algebra is governed by sums of path weights in the graph, and binary expansions appear because ei2e_{i}^{2} doubles the degree; turning this into a proof of the “only if” part requires controlling cancellations, which we could not do.
